teile.einleitung: Intershops were shops in the GDR where you could buy Western goods. However, you did not pay with the GDR mark but with Western money such as the Deutschmark. In this way the state obtained badly needed foreign currency.
wichtigste: The Intershop trading company was founded on 14 December 1962.
The first sales stands were at Friedrichstrasse station in East Berlin.
Payment was made with freely convertible money such as the Deutschmark.
From 1974 GDR citizens were allowed to own Western money legally.
From 1979 GDR citizens had to pay in the Intershop with Forum cheques.
In 1988 there were 416 Intershop shops.

abschnitte.text: In an **Intershop** only **freely convertible money** was accepted, such as the **Deutschmark**, the currency of West Germany. The GDR mark was not accepted. The state needed such money, known as **foreign currency**, to buy goods and machines in the West. From 1985 the Intershops took more than a billion Deutschmarks a year.

The Intershop trading company was founded on **14 December 1962**. The first sales stands were at **Friedrichstrasse station** in East Berlin. This station was a border crossing between East and West. At first it was mainly cigarettes that were sold to travellers from the West.

Until 1974 GDR citizens were forbidden to own Western money. But many received money from relatives in the West. From **1974** owning it was allowed, and they could shop in most Intershops. From April **1979** they first had to exchange their Deutschmarks for **Forum cheques**. Only with these vouchers could they go on shopping in the Intershop.

The Intershop sold goods from the West that were otherwise hardly available in the GDR. These included **chocolate** and other sweets, **cosmetics**, clothes, coffee and electronics. The number of shops grew from 271 in the 1970s to **416** in 1988. They were found in towns, on motorways and at border crossings.

The Intershops caused resentment in the GDR. People with relatives in the West could buy nice things; others could not. This created a kind of two-class society. At the same time the full shelves showed how much there was in the West and how scarce many things were in the GDR.

gewusst: Many people from the GDR still remember the typical smell of soap, coffee and perfume in the Intershops.

teile.einleitung: Eurocommunism is the name for a trend among communist parties in Western Europe in the 1970s. These parties wanted to achieve socialism by democratic means and broke away from the example of the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The most important Eurocommunist parties were the Italian and the Spanish Communist Parties.
Enrico Berlinguer led the Italian Communist Party (PCI) from 1972 to 1984.
After the military coup in Chile in 1973, Berlinguer proposed the “historic compromise” with the Christian Democrats.
In 1976 the PCI achieved its best election result with 34.4 per cent.
The Eurocommunists gave up the dictatorship of the proletariat.
In 1977 Santiago Carrillo wrote the book “Eurocommunism and the State”.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the Soviet Union demanded that all communist parties follow its model. This included the **dictatorship of the proletariat**, meaning the rule of a single party in the name of the workers. The Eurocommunists gave up this idea. They wanted to keep elections, several parties and basic rights. They wanted to achieve socialism through majorities in parliament.

The **Italian Communist Party** was the largest communist party in Western Europe. From 1972 it was led by **Enrico Berlinguer** as general secretary. In 1976 it won 34.4 per cent of the vote and was only just over four percentage points behind the Christian Democrats. In the same year Berlinguer said in an interview that he felt safer under the protection of **NATO**. With this he clearly distanced himself from Moscow.

In 1973 the military in Chile overthrew the elected left-wing government of Salvador Allende. Berlinguer concluded from this that a left-wing government with a narrow majority can fail. He therefore proposed the **historic compromise**, a cooperation between communists and Christian Democrats. His most important partner was the Christian Democrat **Aldo Moro**. In 1978 Moro was kidnapped and killed by the terrorist group the Red Brigades. With that the compromise lost its most important supporter.

Eurocommunism also developed in Spain. **Santiago Carrillo**, general secretary of the Communist Party of Spain, published the book “Eurocommunism and the State” in 1977. In it he explained the break with the Soviet model. The French communists also moved closer to the movement for a time, but stayed closer to Moscow.

On 7 June 1984 Berlinguer suffered a stroke during an election speech in Padua and died a few days later. Hundreds of thousands came to his funeral. After his death Eurocommunism lost momentum. After the end of the communist states in Eastern Europe, the PCI changed its name in 1991 and became a social democratic party.

gewusst: Berlinguer came from Sassari on the island of Sardinia.
In Italian the historic compromise is called “compromesso storico”.

teile.einleitung: The Hundred Flowers Campaign was a political campaign in China in 1956 and 1957. The Communist Party under Mao Zedong called on people to criticise openly. Shortly afterwards many critics were harshly punished.
wichtigste: The campaign took place from 1956 to 1957.
The slogan was “Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend”.
Intellectuals were invited to criticise the party and the administration openly.
The criticism was harsher than expected, and in the summer of 1957 the campaign was stopped.
It was followed by the Anti-Rightist Campaign, in which officially around 550,000 people were labelled “rightists”.

abschnitte.text: In 1956 **Mao Zedong** called for an open discussion. The slogan was: “**Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend.**” The second part refers to the “**Hundred Schools of Thought**” in ancient China. During the **Warring States** period many schools of thought arose, such as Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism. So what was meant was a contest of opinions.

The party leadership above all invited **intellectuals** to speak openly about problems in the party and administration. Intellectuals are people who work with their knowledge, for example teachers, professors and writers. In the spring of 1957 many expressed their opinions, in newspapers and on wall posters. The criticism was much harsher than the party had expected. In the summer of 1957 the campaign was stopped.

It was immediately followed by the **Anti-Rightist Campaign**. Many critics were now branded as “**rightists**”, that is, as enemies of socialism. According to official figures this affected around 550,000 people; some historians estimate the number to be higher. Many lost their jobs or were sent to labour camps. The campaign was largely organised by **Deng Xiaoping**, who later became a reformer.

After this experience, many people in China did not dare to criticise openly for a long time. It is still debated today whether Mao deliberately wanted to lure the critics out or whether he was surprised by how strong the criticism was. After 1978 most of those affected were **rehabilitated**. This means their condemnation was officially recognised as unjust.

gewusst: Of all people, it was Deng Xiaoping, who led the Anti-Rightist Campaign, who later made sure that many of those affected were rehabilitated.

teile.einleitung: From 1928 the Soviet Union under Stalin built up a large industry in a very short time. The state planned everything, from steelworks to power stations. The successes were great, but millions of people paid for them with hardship and forced labour.
wichtigste: From 1928 five-year plans steered the economy.
In a planned economy the state sets production and prices.
The state planning authority was called Gosplan.
Heavy industry, meaning steel, coal and machines, had priority.
From 1929 Magnitogorsk in the Urals was built around a huge steelworks.
Many major building sites were built by prisoners from the Gulag camps.

abschnitte.text: In a **planned economy** the state decides what is made, how much and at what price. Supply and demand hardly play a role. From 1928 the Soviet Union set its targets in **five-year plans**. The planning authority **Gosplan** calculated what each enterprise had to achieve. The first five-year plan was officially declared fulfilled after just over four years.

Stalin wanted to make the country strong quickly, militarily too. That is why **heavy industry** had priority: steel, coal, machines and weapons. Everyday goods such as clothes, shoes or furniture remained scarce. Many people lived in cramped flats and had to queue for a long time.

From 1929 the town of **Magnitogorsk** was built in the **Urals**. It grew up near Magnetic Mountain, which contained a lot of iron ore, around a huge steelworks. On the **Dnieper** river in Ukraine, the **Dneproges** hydroelectric power station went into operation in 1932; it was one of the largest of its time. Projects like these became symbols of Soviet industrialisation.

In 1935 the miner **Alexei Stakhanov** dug many times the prescribed amount of coal in a single shift. The party made him a role model for all workers. The **Stakhanovite movement**, which was meant to spur workers on to ever new records, was named after him. For many workers, however, this also meant higher quotas.

Many major building sites were built with **forced labour**. The **White Sea-Baltic Canal** was built from 1931 to 1933 almost entirely by prisoners from the **Gulag** camps. Many thousands died from cold, hunger and exhaustion. At the same time the peasants were forced to hand over their farms to collective farms. This led to severe famines in the early 1930s.

gewusst: Magnitogorsk was planned on the model of the steelworks in Gary in the USA, and American firms helped to build it.
In his record shift Stakhanov dug around 102 tonnes of coal, about fourteen times the quota.

teile.einleitung: Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary and politician who led the revolution in Cuba in 1959. After that he ruled the Caribbean island as its communist leader for almost 50 years. To some he was a hero who fought against the USA; to others he was a dictator who allowed no freedom.
wichtigste: Fidel Castro lived from 1926 to 2016.
In 1959 he led the revolution in Cuba and overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista.
He ruled Cuba as its communist leader for many decades.
Under him Cuba became an ally of the Soviet Union.
In 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba led to the dangerous Cuban Missile Crisis.
Education and healthcare became free for everyone, but there were no free elections.
In 2008 he handed power to his brother Raúl Castro.

abschnitte.text: Fidel Castro was born in **1926** in Birán in the east of Cuba, the son of a rich landowner. He went to Jesuit schools and studied law in Havana. He was already very active in politics as a student. At that time Cuba was ruled by the dictator **Fulgencio Batista**, and many people in the countryside were very poor.

On 26 July 1953 Castro and a small group attacked the **Moncada Barracks**, but the attack failed and he went to prison. After his release he went to Mexico, where he met **Che Guevara**. At the end of 1956 they landed in Cuba on the small boat **Granma** and waged a guerrilla war from the mountains of the Sierra Maestra. On 1 January 1959 Batista fled, and the revolutionaries marched into Havana.

Castro nationalised companies and land, including American property. The USA then imposed a **trade embargo**, which still exists today. In 1961 an attack by Cuban exiles supported by the USA failed at the **Bay of Pigs**. In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles in Cuba, and during the **Cuban Missile Crisis** the world came close to nuclear war.

Castro built up a free school and healthcare system, and almost all Cubans learned to read and write. At the same time only one party was allowed, the **Communist Party of Cuba**. Newspapers were controlled, and critics were sent to prison. Hundreds of thousands of people fled to the USA, especially to Florida.

Castro was prime minister from 1959 to 1976 and then president of Cuba until 2008. Because of a serious illness he handed power to his brother **Raúl Castro**, temporarily in 2006 and for good in **2008**. He died in Havana on 25 November **2016**. Opinions about him still differ greatly today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rapid, often violent overthrow of a government and the order of society.
Small armed groups that fight against an army from hiding places.
A ban on trading with a particular country.
A dangerous dispute between the USA and the Soviet Union in October 1962 over nuclear missiles in Cuba.

gewusst: Fidel Castro sometimes gave speeches that lasted several hours.
From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba, because the two countries had no embassies in each other's country.
In public Castro almost always wore an olive-green uniform and a beard.

teile.einleitung: John Paul II was Pope from 1978 to 2005 and thus head of the Catholic Church. He came from Poland and his real name was Karol Wojtyła. He played an important part in the end of communism in Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: Karol Wojtyła was born in Wadowice in Poland in 1920.
On 16 October 1978 he was elected Pope.
He was the first Pope in more than 450 years who was not Italian.
In 1979 he visited his home country of Poland for the first time as Pope.
On 13 May 1981 he survived an assassination attempt in St Peter's Square.
He died on 2 April 2005, and in 2014 he was declared a saint.

abschnitte.text: **Karol Wojtyła** was born in **Wadowice** in Poland in 1920. He became a priest and later **Archbishop of Kraków**. On **16 October 1978** the cardinals elected him Pope, and he took the name **John Paul II**. Since 1523 all Popes had been Italian. The fact that a Pole from a communist country was now Pope caused a sensation around the world.

In June **1979** the Pope travelled to Poland for the first time in his new role. Millions of people came to his Masses. At that time Poland was governed by a communist party, which watched the Church with suspicion. The visit gave many Poles new courage. Shortly afterwards the free trade union **Solidarność** was formed, and the Pope supported it.

On **13 May 1981** the attacker Mehmet Ali Ağca shot the Pope in **St Peter's Square** in Rome and seriously injured him. John Paul II survived. Later he visited his attacker in prison and talked with him. Many people saw this as a sign of reconciliation.

In the Vatican he was protected by the **Pontifical Swiss Guard**, which has guarded the Pope since 1506. Its soldiers are young Catholic Swiss men. John Paul II visited Switzerland several times. In June **2004**, already seriously ill, he travelled to **Bern** and met thousands of young people there. It was his last trip to Switzerland.

John Paul II travelled to more than a hundred countries, more than any Pope before him. In 1989 communist rule ended in Poland and other countries of Eastern Europe. Many historians see him as one of those who paved the way for this change. He died in Rome on **2 April 2005**. In **2014** he was **declared a saint**.

gewusst: As a young man Karol Wojtyła acted in the theatre and wrote poems.
At more than 26 years, his time in office is one of the longest of all Popes.

teile.einleitung: Kim Il-sung was the founder and first ruler of North Korea. He ruled the country as a dictator from 1948 until his death in 1994. He is still worshipped like a hero in North Korea today.
wichtigste: Kim Il-sung was born on 15 April 1912.
With the help of the Soviet Union he came to power after the Second World War.
In 1948 North Korea was founded, and Kim Il-sung became head of government.
In 1950 he started the Korean War with an attack on the south.
He ruled until his death in 1994.
His son Kim Jong-il succeeded him as ruler.
There is a huge cult of personality around him in North Korea.

abschnitte.text: Until 1945 Korea was occupied by Japan. After the **Second World War** the **Soviet Union** occupied the north and the USA the south. The Soviet Union supported Kim Il-sung as leader in the north. On **9 September 1948** the **Democratic People's Republic of Korea**, that is, North Korea, was founded. Kim Il-sung became its first head of government.

In **June 1950** North Korea attacked the south. This started the **Korean War**. UN troops led by the USA helped South Korea, and China supported the north. The war cost a great many lives. In 1953 it ended with a **ceasefire**, but without a peace treaty. That is why Korea is still divided today.

Kim Il-sung ruled North Korea as a **dictator** for almost **46 years**. There were no free elections and no freedom of opinion. After his death in July **1994**, his son **Kim Jong-il** took power. Today his grandson, **Kim Jong-un**, is already in charge. In 1998 Kim Il-sung was declared **“Eternal President”** in the constitution.

There is a huge **cult of personality** around Kim Il-sung. This is an exaggerated worship of a person. All over the country there are statues and pictures of him, and people must bow before his monuments. His birthday on **15 April** is celebrated as the **“Day of the Sun”**. His embalmed body lies in the **Kumsusan Palace** in **Pyongyang**.

gewusst: The Kumsusan Palace used to be Kim Il-sung's official residence and was turned into a mausoleum after his death.
His son and successor Kim Jong-il also lies in the Kumsusan Palace today.

teile.einleitung: Josip Broz Tito was a Yugoslav partisan leader and politician who ruled Yugoslavia from 1945 to 1980. He ran the country as a communist state but stayed independent of the Soviet Union. This gave Yugoslavia a special position among the communist states.
wichtigste: Josip Broz Tito lived from 1892 to 1980.
In the Second World War he led the partisans in the fight against the German and Italian occupiers.
From 1945 he ruled Yugoslavia, and from 1953 as president.
In 1948 he broke with Stalin, and Yugoslavia stayed independent of the Soviet Union.
He was one of the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement.
Yugoslavs were allowed to travel abroad, and many worked in Switzerland or Germany.
After his death Yugoslavia broke up into several states in the 1990s.

abschnitte.text: Josip Broz was born in **1892** in **Kumrovec** in what is now Croatia, which at that time belonged to Austria-Hungary. He trained as a locksmith and worked in various countries, including in factories in Germany and Austria. In the First World War he was taken prisoner by the Russians and experienced the revolution there. Back in Yugoslavia he became a communist and later called himself **Tito**.

In 1941 Germany and Italy occupied Yugoslavia. Tito led the communist **partisans**, who fought against the occupiers in the mountains. The war was very cruel, and different ethnic groups in Yugoslavia also fought each other. In 1945 the partisans liberated the country largely by their own efforts.

After the war Tito became head of a communist **Yugoslavia** made up of six republics. But he did not want **Stalin** to tell him how to govern. In 1948 there was a break, and Yugoslavia was expelled from the alliance of communist parties. After that the country went **its own way** and later did not join the Warsaw Pact either.

Instead of a pure planned economy, Tito introduced **workers' self-management**, in which the workforce partly helped to run their enterprises. In 1961 he hosted the first conference of **Non-Aligned States** in Belgrade; these countries wanted to belong neither to the West nor to the East. Yugoslavs were free to travel, and many went to Germany, Austria and **Switzerland** as guest workers. Even so, Yugoslavia was a one-party dictatorship in which opponents were locked up, for example on the prison island of Goli Otok.

Tito died in Ljubljana on 4 May **1980**, and state guests from all over the world came to his funeral. He is buried in the **House of Flowers** in Belgrade. Without him the tensions between the ethnic groups grew stronger. In the 1990s Yugoslavia broke up in bloody wars into several states, such as Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fighters who do not belong to a regular army and fight against occupiers.
Countries that did not want to join either the West or the East during the Cold War.
People who went to another country to work, for example to Switzerland.
A state in south-eastern Europe that existed from 1918 until the 1990s.

gewusst: In 1974 Tito was named president for life.
Representatives from more than 120 states came to Tito's funeral in 1980.
In many towns of the former Yugoslavia, streets and squares still bear Tito's name today.

teile.einleitung: The Commonwealth of Independent States, CIS for short, is an association of former Soviet republics. It was formed in December 1991, when the Soviet Union broke up.
wichtigste: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus founded the CIS in December 1991.
On 21 December 1991 eight more republics joined in Alma-Ata.
At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union officially dissolved.
The CIS has its seat in Minsk, the capital of Belarus.
The Baltic states never joined the CIS.
Georgia left after its war with Russia; its withdrawal took effect in 2009.

abschnitte.text: In December 1991 the leaders of **Russia**, **Ukraine** and **Belarus** signed an agreement founding the CIS. It was drawn up in Belarus, not far from **Minsk**. With it they declared the Soviet Union to be over. On 21 December 1991 in **Alma-Ata**, today's Almaty in Kazakhstan, eleven former Soviet republics signed a joint declaration.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: On 25 December 1991 **Mikhail Gorbachev** resigned as president of the Soviet Union. The next day the Soviet Union officially dissolved. **Russia** was recognised as the **continuing state**. It took over the Soviet Union's permanent seat on the **UN Security Council**, its embassies and its nuclear weapons.

abschnitte.titel: Who is in and who is not
abschnitte.text: The Baltic states of **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania** never joined. They saw themselves as occupied countries and sought to join the EU and NATO. **Georgia** announced its withdrawal after the war over South Ossetia in 2008, and this took effect in 2009. **Turkmenistan** downgraded its membership to associate status in 2005 because it sees itself as permanently neutral. **Ukraine** never ratified the CIS Charter and ended its participation in the bodies in 2018.

The CIS is meant to make cooperation in the economy, transport and security easier. Its **Executive Committee** has its seat in Minsk. In 1992 several states signed the Collective Security Treaty in **Tashkent**. In 2002 this gave rise to a military alliance around Russia, to which only some CIS states belong. Overall the CIS is more of a loose association than a firm union.

gewusst: In December 1991 the founders of the CIS met in a hunting lodge in a large forest area in Belarus.
Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality has been recognised by the UN since 1995.

teile.einleitung: Historical materialism is the view of history held by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. According to this theory, it is mainly economic conditions that determine how a society develops. History is understood as a series of class struggles.
wichtigste: The term “historical materialism” was made popular by Friedrich Engels; Marx himself did not use it.
According to the “Communist Manifesto”, the history of all society so far is a history of class struggles.
Marx took over dialectics from Hegel but put material conditions first.
According to Marx, when the productive forces come into conflict with the relations of production, an era of social revolution begins.
In the classic scheme, feudalism is followed by capitalism.
A short summary can be found in the preface to “A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy” (1859).

abschnitte.text: In everyday life, “materialistic” means that someone cares a lot about possessions. In philosophy, **materialism** means something different: people's real, material living conditions come first, and ideas follow from them. Marx believed that the way people work and make goods shapes their thinking, their laws and their politics. The term **historical materialism** was used mainly by **Friedrich Engels** from around 1890, and after that it became established.

The philosopher **Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel** described history as a **dialectical** development of the mind or spirit. Dialectics means that something new develops through opposites and the overcoming of them. Marx and Engels took over this method but wanted to “turn it upside down” in a materialist way. For them it is not ideas that develop, but economic and social conditions.

abschnitte.titel: Productive forces and relations of production
abschnitte.text: The **productive forces** include tools, machines and people's skills. The **relations of production** describe who owns the factories and the land and who works for whom. According to Marx, when the productive forces grow, at some point they burst the old relations apart. Then an **era of social revolution** begins. Marx briefly summed up these ideas in 1859 in the preface to “A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy”.

The “Communist Manifesto” of 1848 says: the history of all society so far is the history of **class struggles**. In the classic scheme the forms of society follow one another: **primitive society**, **slave society**, **feudalism**, **capitalism** and finally socialism or communism. Whether history really follows such a plan is very much disputed among historians.

As early as 1845 Marx wrote the short “**Theses on Feuerbach**”. The eleventh thesis says that philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it. In 1845 and 1846 Marx and Engels wrote “**The German Ideology**” together. In it they set out their view of history in detail for the first time. The complete work was not published until 1932.

gewusst: Marx and Engels could not find a publisher for “The German Ideology” and, in their own words, left the manuscript “to the gnawing criticism of the mice”.
Today the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach is written in large letters in the entrance hall of the Humboldt University in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: The secret files scandal shook Switzerland in 1989. It came out that for decades the Federal Police had secretly kept index cards on hundreds of thousands of people and organisations.
wichtigste: “Fichen” are index cards on which the Federal Police collected notes about people.
Around 900,000 such cards were found.
During the Cold War, it was mainly people thought to be left-wing or communist who were watched.
The cards were discovered by a parliamentary commission of inquiry (PUK) led by Moritz Leuenberger.
On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the “snooping state”.
More than 300,000 people asked to see their own file card.

abschnitte.text: The word **“Fiche”** comes from French and means index card. The **Federal Police** had made such cards about many people and organisations. They contained notes, for example about meetings people had attended, journeys or contacts. The people concerned knew nothing about it. More than 700,000 people and organisations were recorded.

In January 1989 **Elisabeth Kopp**, the first woman Federal Councillor in Switzerland, resigned. Parliament then set up a **parliamentary commission of inquiry**, PUK for short. It examined how the Federal Department of Justice and Police was being run, in particular the work against money laundering and drug trafficking. In doing so it came across a large room full of file cards. The chairman of the PUK was National Councillor **Moritz Leuenberger**, who was elected to the Federal Council in 1995.

During the **Cold War**, many people feared the influence of the Soviet Union. **State security** therefore mainly kept watch on left-wingers, trade unionists, peace activists and people from abroad. Harmless activities were often enough for an entry, such as taking part in a demonstration. Much of the information was unimportant or even wrong.

The discovery caused great outrage. On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people in **Bern** protested against the so-called **snooping state**. It was one of the largest demonstrations of that time in Switzerland. More than 300,000 people made a request to **see** their file card. They received copies in which the names of other people had often been blacked out.

The scandal changed Swiss politics. Parliament demanded better **oversight** of state security. Later new laws were passed that set out more precisely whom and what the state may watch. How much surveillance is needed to protect the country is still being debated in Switzerland today.

gewusst: The writer Max Frisch also had a file card.
When they read them, many of the people concerned found that their file card contained only very ordinary or wrong information.

teile.einleitung: Unofficial collaborators, IM for short, were the secret informers of the GDR's State Security. They reported on people around them without those people knowing. In this way the Stasi kept watch on large parts of the population.
wichtigste: IM stands for “Inoffizieller Mitarbeiter”, unofficial collaborator of the Ministry for State Security.
In 1989 there were around 189,000 active IMs.
On top of these there were more than 90,000 full-time Stasi employees.
The Stasi saw itself as the “shield and sword of the party”.
Erich Mielke was Minister for State Security from 1957 to 1989.
The first head of the authority for the Stasi records was Joachim Gauck.

abschnitte.text: The **Ministry for State Security**, **Stasi** for short, was the secret police of the GDR. Besides its permanent staff, it used **unofficial collaborators**. These were quite ordinary people who secretly reported on colleagues, neighbours, friends and even family members. Some took part out of conviction, others for advantages or because they were put under pressure. In 1989 there were around **189,000** active IMs.

abschnitte.titel: Shield and sword of the party
abschnitte.text: The Stasi saw itself as the “**shield and sword of the party**”. So it served above all to **keep the SED in power**. From 1957 to 1989 **Erich Mielke** led the ministry and expanded it greatly. Foreign espionage was led for a long time by **Markus Wolf**. By the end the Stasi had more than 90,000 full-time employees.

In the autumn of 1989 the SED's power collapsed. On 13 November 1989 Mielke spoke in front of the **People's Chamber**, the GDR's parliament. When members booed him, he called out: “Ich liebe doch alle, alle Menschen.” This means “But I love all, all people.” After decades of surveillance this sentence seemed grotesque and was laughed at.

The Stasi headquarters were on **Normannenstrasse** in Berlin-Lichtenberg. On **15 January 1990** demonstrators stormed the site. They wanted to stop the files from being destroyed. Today it houses the **Stasi Museum**, where you can visit Mielke's office, for example.

After reunification an authority was created for the **Stasi records**. Its first head, from 1990 to 2000, was **Joachim Gauck**, so it was popularly called the “**Gauck authority**”. Gauck later became Federal President of Germany. Since 1992 the people affected have been able to read their own files. In this way many found out who had spied on them.

gewusst: If all the Stasi files were placed side by side on shelves, they would stretch more than 100 kilometres.
At the end of 1989 Stasi staff tried to tear up files. Today the scraps are painstakingly being put back together.

teile.einleitung: A five-year plan is a state economic plan that sets out what is to be produced over the next five years. The Soviet Union introduced the first such plan in 1928 in order to become an industrial country quickly. Later many other countries, such as China or the GDR, took over this idea.
wichtigste: A five-year plan is a state economic plan with production targets for five years.
The Soviet Union's first five-year plan began in 1928 under Joseph Stalin.
An authority called Gosplan worked out how much each factory should make.
Above all, the amount of steel, coal, machines and electricity was meant to grow quickly.
At the same time farms were forcibly merged into large collectives.
Industry grew strongly, but many people suffered from hunger and forced labour.
China still works with five-year plans today.

abschnitte.text: In a **planned economy** it is not the market but the state that decides what is made. A **five-year plan** sets exact targets for this, for example how many tonnes of steel or how many tractors are to be produced. Each factory receives its own quota, which it has to meet. The state also sets prices and wages.

The first five-year plan ran from **1928** and was declared fulfilled after just over four years, at the end of 1932. Joseph Stalin wanted to turn the Soviet Union from a farming country into an **industrial country** as fast as possible. Huge steelworks were built, such as in **Magnitogorsk**, as well as dams, canals and tractor factories. At the same time agriculture was violently **collectivised**.

The production of steel, coal and electricity rose sharply. But many targets were far too high, and figures were often made to look better to avoid punishment. Quantity often mattered more than quality, so many goods were poor. Many large building projects were built by **prisoners from the Gulag**, and in the countryside there were severe famines.

After the Second World War many communist countries took over the idea, for example the **GDR**, Poland and China. China started its first five-year plan in 1953 and still uses such plans today, though together with a market economy. India also had five-year plans from 1951 to 2017, even though it is not a communist country. There they were more about targets for roads, schools and agriculture.

Switzerland has a **market economy**, in which companies decide for themselves what they make and at what price they sell it. The state sets rules but does not plan all production. Even so, Switzerland also has plans for individual areas, such as expanding the railway. These set out where money is invested, but not how many shoes or loaves of bread are made.

begriffe.erklaerung: An economic system in which the state decides what is produced and what it costs.
An economic system in which supply and demand determine prices and production.
Merging many farms into large enterprises owned by the state or the community.
The state planning authority of the Soviet Union.

gewusst: In the Soviet Union there was a slogan that you should fulfil the five-year plan in four years.
In 1935 the miner Alexei Stakhanov is said to have mined much more coal than usual in one shift, and he was celebrated as a hero for it.
Because factories were judged by weight, some deliberately made especially heavy products.

teile.einleitung: The International Workingmen's Association was the first large alliance of workers across national borders. It was founded in London in 1864 and is also known as the First International. Several of its congresses took place in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The International Workingmen's Association was founded in London on 28 September 1864.
It is also called the First International, because others followed later.
Karl Marx wrote the Inaugural Address, its founding declaration.
The first congress took place in Geneva in 1866, and in 1869 delegates met in Basel.
In 1872 the anarchist Mikhail Bakunin was expelled.
After that the General Council moved to New York, and the organisation lost importance.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many people worked in factories under harsh conditions. Workers' representatives from several European countries therefore wanted to join forces. On **28 September 1864** they founded the **International Workingmen's Association** in St Martin's Hall in **London**. Because other international workers' alliances were formed later, it is called the **First International**.

abschnitte.titel: Karl Marx on the General Council
abschnitte.text: **Karl Marx** sat on the **General Council**, the organisation's leadership, and wrote its most important declarations. The **Inaugural Address**, the founding declaration, was written by him. But the members were very different from each other. There were trade unionists, socialists and anarchists, who often had different aims.

Because of its freedoms, Switzerland was a popular meeting place. In 1866 the first congress took place in **Geneva**. The delegates discussed working hours and workers' rights. Further congresses followed in **Lausanne** and in 1869 in **Basel**, where around 75 delegates met. In Basel the ideas of the anarchists found a lot of support.

The Russian anarchist **Mikhail Bakunin** rejected every kind of state. Marx, by contrast, believed that the workers first had to win power in the state. The dispute grew more and more bitter. In 1872, at the congress in **The Hague**, Marx's supporters won the day, and Bakunin was expelled. So as not to leave the leadership to the anarchists, the General Council was moved to **New York**.

The **Jura Federation**, a group of watchmakers and workers in the Jura, rejected the decisions of The Hague. A week later anarchists gathered in **Saint-Imier** in the Bernese Jura for a rival congress. The meeting is seen as the birth of the anarchist International. In New York the First International soon lost importance, and it dissolved in 1876.

gewusst: Many of Bakunin's supporters in the Jura were watchmakers who worked in small workshops.
In 2012 the 1872 meeting was celebrated in Saint-Imier with a large international anarchist gathering.

teile.einleitung: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space. On 12 April 1961 the cosmonaut from the Soviet Union orbited the Earth once and became world-famous.
wichtigste: Yuri Gagarin was born in a small village in Russia in 1934.
He was a pilot in the Soviet air force.
On 12 April 1961 he became the first person to fly into space.
He took off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
Gagarin orbited the Earth once; the flight lasted about 108 minutes.
At take-off he called out “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let's go!”.
Since 2011, 12 April has been a UN day of remembrance.

abschnitte.text: Yuri Gagarin was born in **1934** in a small village west of Moscow. His parents worked on a farm. As a teenager he did an apprenticeship and began flying at a flying club. Later he became a **pilot** in the Soviet air force. In 1960 he and other young pilots were chosen to train as space travellers.

On **12 April 1961** Gagarin took off in the spacecraft **Vostok 1** from the **Baikonur** Cosmodrome on the steppe of Kazakhstan. At take-off he called out “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let's go!”. He orbited the Earth **exactly once**. From take-off to landing the flight lasted about **108 minutes**, just under two hours. Gagarin was 27 years old at the time.

Space travellers from the Soviet Union and Russia are called **cosmonauts**. In the USA they say **astronaut**, and in China **taikonaut**. All these words mean roughly the same thing: a person who travels into space. Gagarin's flight took place in the middle of the **Cold War**. At that time the Soviet Union and the USA were in a race into space, and the Soviet Union was faster with the first crewed flight.

abschnitte.titel: A hero all over the world
abschnitte.text: After his return Gagarin was celebrated as a **hero** in the Soviet Union. He travelled to many countries and was greeted everywhere by large crowds. He never flew into space again. In 1968 he was killed during a training flight in a fighter jet. Since 2011, **12 April** has been the UN's **International Day of Human Space Flight**.

gewusst: Before Gagarin, the satellite Sputnik 1 had already been launched into space from Baikonur in 1957.
After his death Gagarin's home town of Gzhatsk was renamed “Gagarin”.
In Russia 12 April is “Cosmonautics Day” every year.

teile.einleitung: The Free German Youth, FDJ for short, was the state youth organisation of the GDR. Almost all young people in eastern Germany were members. The FDJ was closely linked to the ruling party, the SED.
wichtigste: The FDJ was founded on 7 March 1946 in the Soviet occupation zone.
It was the only state-recognised youth organisation in the GDR.
You could become a member from the age of 14, officially on a voluntary basis.
Its trademarks were the blue shirt and a badge with a rising sun.
The official greeting was “Freundschaft!” (Friendship!).
Its first chairman, from 1946 to 1955, was Erich Honecker.

abschnitte.text: The FDJ was founded on **7 March 1946** in the **Soviet occupation zone**, which became the GDR in 1949. It was meant to bring up young people in the spirit of socialism. Its first chairman was **Erich Honecker**, who later became head of state and party leader of the GDR. The FDJ was the only state-recognised youth organisation; there were hardly any other independent youth groups.

At official events the members wore a **blue shirt**, and girls a blue blouse. It was called the **blue shirt** (“Blauhemd”). The badge, a yellow **rising sun** on a blue background, was sewn onto the sleeve. The sun stood for a new beginning and a bright future. At meetings and roll calls people greeted each other with “Freundschaft!”.

abschnitte.titel: From the Pioneers to the FDJ
abschnitte.text: Younger children belonged to the **Pioneers**, who had their own greeting. At **14** most young people moved on to the FDJ. Membership was officially voluntary. But those who did not join often faced disadvantages, for example when choosing an apprenticeship or a university place. The FDJ organised leisure activities, holiday camps, sport and political training.

The FDJ's daily newspaper was called “**Junge Welt**” (Young World). It had the highest circulation of all daily newspapers in the GDR and is still published today. In the **People's Chamber**, the GDR's parliament, the FDJ had its own **parliamentary group**. The seats were shared out in advance through the single list of the National Front. In this way all parliamentary groups stayed under the control of the SED.

In 1973 the **World Festival of Youth and Students** took place in **East Berlin**. Young people came from many countries, and the FDJ organised the big festival. For many young people in the GDR it was a rare chance to meet guests from all over the world. After the end of the GDR in 1990, the FDJ lost almost all its members.

gewusst: Egon Krenz, who briefly became Honecker's successor in 1989, had also once been head of the FDJ.
The newspaper “Junge Welt” has existed since 1947.

teile.einleitung: Capitalism is an economic system in which factories and companies belong to private owners. They want to make a profit with their companies. Many countries today, including Switzerland, have an economy with the main features of capitalism.
wichtigste: In capitalism, companies and factories belong to private owners.
Workers receive a wage for their work.
Companies want to make as much profit as possible.
Capital is the money, machines and buildings used to run a company.
An entrepreneur founds and runs a company and bears the risk.
Karl Marx was the best-known critic of capitalism.

abschnitte.text: In capitalism, factories, shops and machines belong to **private owners**. These can be individual people or companies with many shareholders. The owners decide what is made in their company. Most people do not own a factory. They work for a company and receive a **wage** for it.

The word **capital** means money, machines or buildings used to run a company. Capitalism gets its name from it. Someone who founds and runs a company is called an **entrepreneur**. The aim is **profit**: the money left over when all costs have been paid. If things go badly, though, the entrepreneur can also lose money.

Many companies offer similar goods and are in **competition**. Each wants to be better or cheaper than the others. That is why many people say an advantage of capitalism is that there is a **wide choice of goods**. Competition can also lead to new inventions. The Scot **Adam Smith** described such ideas as early as the 18th century.

The best-known critic of capitalism was **Karl Marx**. He believed that the workers create the value of goods with their work, but the owners keep the profit. In this way the owners would become rich and the workers would stay poor. He thought this was **unfair**. Marx therefore wanted a different system, **communism**, in which everything belongs to everyone together.

Today there is hardly any country with pure capitalism. In Switzerland and many other countries the state makes **rules** for companies, for example to protect workers. There are also social insurance schemes such as the **AHV** (old-age insurance). The right mix of freedom for companies and rules from the state is often argued about in politics.

gewusst: The word “capital” comes from the Latin word “caput”, which means “head”.
Karl Marx simply called his most famous book “Capital”.

teile.einleitung: The hammer and sickle are two crossed tools that together form the best-known symbol of communism. They stand for the workers in the factories and the peasants in the countryside. The sign was on the flag of the Soviet Union and is still known all over the world today.
wichtigste: The hammer and sickle are a symbol of communism.
The hammer stands for the workers, the sickle for the peasants.
Together they show the alliance of these two groups.
The symbol was created in 1917 and 1918 after the Russian Revolution.
From 1923 it appeared on the flag of the Soviet Union.
Many communist parties around the world still use it today.
In some Eastern European countries displaying the symbol in public is banned.

abschnitte.text: A **hammer** is a tool used by blacksmiths, craftspeople and factory workers. A **sickle** is a curved blade that people used in the past to cut grain. In the symbol the two tools lie crossed over each other. They are usually shown in yellow or gold on a red background.

The hammer stands for the **workers** in the towns, the sickle for the **peasants** in the countryside. According to communist teaching, these two groups were to take power together. They were seen as the people whose work produces everything a society needs. So the sign was meant to show that the state belongs to working people.

The symbol was created after the **Russian Revolution** of 1917. From 1918 it appeared in the coat of arms of the new Soviet Republic of Russia. With the founding of the **Soviet Union** it became part of the red state flag in 1923, together with a star. Communist parties in many countries soon took over the sign.

Other communist states chose their own similar symbols. The **GDR** had a hammer and a pair of compasses inside a wreath of ears of corn in its coat of arms; the compasses stood for scholars. The Workers' Party of Korea in North Korea shows a hammer, a sickle and a brush. The flag of **Angola** shows a cogwheel and a machete.

For some people the symbol stands for justice and the workers' struggle. For many others it is a reminder of **dictatorship**, persecution and camps in communist states. That is why it is banned to display the symbol in public in countries such as Lithuania, Latvia and **Ukraine**. In Switzerland it is allowed, but you rarely see it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture or sign that stands for an idea or a group.
A crescent-shaped blade for cutting grain and grass.
An idea according to which all goods should belong to everyone together.
An emblem that represents a state, a town or a family.

gewusst: The hammer and sickle are even included as a character in many computer fonts and emoji keyboards.
Today the sickle is hardly ever used for harvesting in Switzerland, because combine harvesters do this work.
On the Moon there are Soviet pennants with the hammer and sickle, which were taken there by space probes.

teile.einleitung: Günter Schabowski was a politician of the SED, the ruling party of the GDR. He became famous because of a press conference on 9 November 1989. His words led to the opening of the Berlin Wall that very night.
wichtigste: Schabowski was a member of the Politburo and spokesman for the SED leadership.
On the evening of 9 November 1989 he read out a new travel regulation.
When asked when it would apply, he said: “immediately, without delay”.
The regulation was actually not meant to come into force until 10 November.
That same night the Bornholmer Strasse crossing was the first to be opened.
The Wall had stood for about 28 years.

abschnitte.text: Günter Schabowski was born in 1929 and was a journalist for a long time. He ran the party newspaper “Neues Deutschland” and later became a member of the **Politburo**, the inner leadership of the **SED**. In the autumn of 1989 he was the Central Committee secretary responsible for information. That is why he informed the press about the party's decisions.

In the autumn of 1989 many people in the GDR were protesting, and thousands fled to the West via Hungary. On **9 November 1989** a press conference began at 6 p.m. and was broadcast live on television. Only shortly before 7 p.m. did Schabowski read out a note with a **new travel regulation**. GDR citizens were to be able to apply for trips to the West without needing special reasons.

A journalist asked when the regulation would apply. Schabowski leafed through his papers and answered: “Das tritt nach meiner Kenntnis ist das sofort, unverzüglich.” This muddled sentence means roughly “As far as I know, that comes into effect immediately, without delay.” In fact the regulation was not meant to come into force until **10 November**, with an **embargo** so that everything could run in an orderly way. Schabowski did not know about this embargo. That evening the Western broadcasters reported on it in detail.

After the announcement, thousands of East Berliners streamed to the **border crossings**. At the **Bornholmer Strasse** crossing the crowds were so large that the officer Harald Jäger had the barrier opened at around 11.30 p.m. The other crossings followed. The **Berlin Wall**, which had stood since 13 August 1961, had fallen after about 28 years.

After the end of the GDR, Schabowski was expelled from the party. In 1997 he and other Politburo members were sentenced to prison for the deaths at the border. Unlike many of his former colleagues, he admitted his share of responsibility and clearly criticised the GDR. He died in Berlin in 2015.

gewusst: Schabowski had received the note with the new regulation from Egon Krenz only shortly before the press conference.
Many people heard about the opening of the border not from GDR television but from the Western broadcasters.

teile.einleitung: Ho Chi Minh City is the largest city in Vietnam and lies in the south of the country. Until 1975 it was called Saigon and was the capital of South Vietnam. After the communist victory it was named after the revolutionary leader Ho Chi Minh.
wichtigste: Ho Chi Minh City is Vietnam's largest city and most important economic centre.
Until 1975 the city was called Saigon and was the capital of South Vietnam.
After the communist victory in 1975, Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
The city lies on the Saigon River, not far from the Mekong Delta.
In the 2019 census it had about 9 million inhabitants.
Millions of motor scooters ride through its streets.
Many buildings recall the French colonial period.

abschnitte.text: Ho Chi Minh City lies in the south of **Vietnam** on the **Saigon River**. It is only about 50 kilometres to the South China Sea. South of the city the fertile **Mekong Delta** begins, where a lot of rice is grown. The climate is tropical and warm all year round, with a rainy season from about May to November.

The place was once a village of Khmer fishermen, before Vietnamese people settled there from the 17th century. In the 19th century **France** conquered the city and made Saigon the capital of its colony of Cochinchina. From 1955 Saigon was the capital of **South Vietnam**. After the **Fall of Saigon** on 30 April 1975, the city was renamed after Ho Chi Minh in 1976.

The city is growing fast and is one of the largest cities in South-East Asia. In the 2019 census about **9 million** people lived there, and in 2025 a territorial reform made the city area considerably larger still. Typical are the countless **motor scooters** that flow through the streets in dense streams. Many people still simply call the city, especially the centre, Saigon.

Ho Chi Minh City is Vietnam's most important **economic centre**. It has a large port, many factories, banks and the country's stock exchange. Since Vietnam opened up to the market economy in the 1980s with the **Doi Moi** reform policy, the city has grown rapidly. At the end of 2024 the city's first metro line was opened.

The red-brick **Notre-Dame** Cathedral and the magnificent Central Post Office date from the French period. The Vietnam War ended in the Reunification Palace in 1975. The War Remnants Museum shows how much people suffered in the war. At **Ben Thanh Market** you can buy food, fabrics and souvenirs.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area where a river splits into many branches before it reaches the sea.
The time when a country was ruled by a foreign state, here by France.
Vietnamese for renewal; Vietnam's economic reforms from 1986.
A very large and important city.

gewusst: There are several million motor scooters in Ho Chi Minh City, far more than cars.
The well-known Vietnamese sandwich banh mi has its origins in the French baguette.
On the edge of the city are the Cu Chi tunnels, a huge underground tunnel system from the war.

teile.einleitung: Class struggle is a term from the theory of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. It describes the conflict between social groups that own different amounts and have opposing interests. In capitalism, Marx above all set the workers against the factory owners.
wichtigste: Class struggle is the conflict between different social classes.
The term comes mainly from the writings of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.
In capitalism, Marx set the proletariat, the working class, against the bourgeoisie, the owning class.
The bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and machines.
The proletariat owns nothing except its labour power.
Marx believed that class struggle would eventually lead to a revolution.
In Switzerland the general strike of 1918 was a well-known conflict between the working class and the middle classes.

abschnitte.text: For Marx, a **class** is a large group of people in a similar economic situation. What matters is whether you own **means of production**, that is, factories, machines or land. Those who own them can have others work for them. Those who do not own them have to sell their labour for a wage.

According to Marx, there are two main classes in **capitalism**. The **bourgeoisie** is the owning class of factory owners and entrepreneurs. The **proletariat** is the working class that works in the factories. Marx believed that the owners keep part of the value the workers create and in this way become richer and richer.

In the Communist Manifesto of 1848, Marx and Engels wrote that the history of all societies so far is a history of class struggles. As examples they named free people and slaves in ancient times, or nobles and **serfs** in the Middle Ages. In each case, they said, one group oppressed the other. Marx expected that in the end the workers would win and abolish classes.

In Switzerland too there were hard clashes between the working class and the middle classes. In November **1918**, during the **general strike**, around 250,000 people stopped work and demanded, for example, the 48-hour week and votes for women. The Federal Council sent troops, and the strike was called off after three days. But many demands were met later, such as the AHV old-age insurance in 1948.

Later in Switzerland the path of negotiation won through. In 1937 trade unions and employers in the engineering and metal industry concluded the **Peace Agreement**. In it they promised to settle disputes through talks rather than strikes. This **social partnership**, with collective labour agreements, still shapes the Swiss world of work today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The working class, which owns no factories and works for a wage.
The owning class, which owns factories, companies and capital.
Everything needed to make goods, for example machines, factories and land.
When workers stop working together to achieve better conditions.
The cooperation of trade unions and employers to resolve conflicts through negotiation.

gewusst: The word proletariat comes from ancient Rome, where the poorest citizens were called proletarii.
Compared with other countries, Switzerland has especially few days lost to strikes.
During the general strike of 1918 Switzerland was on the brink of civil war, but only a few people died.

teile.einleitung: Communism is a political idea according to which factories, land and machines should belong to everyone together. There should no longer be rich and poor classes. In the 20th century communist parties ruled many countries, often as strict dictatorships.
wichtigste: The basic idea: factories and land belong to everyone, and there are no rich and poor classes.
The pioneering thinkers were Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the 19th century.
In 1917 communists came to power for the first time, in Russia under Lenin.
Communist states were usually ruled by a single party.
In the Cold War, communist states and Western democracies faced each other.
Communist parties still govern China, Vietnam, Laos and Cuba today.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “communis”, meaning “shared”. In communism there is to be no more **private property** in factories, land and machines. Everyone is to work according to their abilities and receive what they need. This is meant to create a **classless society** in which nobody is rich and nobody is poor.

In 1848 the Germans Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote the “Manifesto of the Communist Party”. They saw how workers in factories toiled for very long hours for low wages. Marx believed that history is a struggle between classes, that is, between owners and workers, the **proletariat**. In the end, he thought, the workers would win and own everything together.

In 1917 Lenin and the Bolsheviks took power in Russia, and in 1922 the **Soviet Union** was formed. After the Second World War many countries in Eastern Europe became communist, and in 1949 so did China under Mao Zedong. These states were ruled by a single party, and there were no free elections. Anyone who disagreed was often persecuted, imprisoned or killed.

The state planned the economy in so-called **planned economies** with five-year plans. Education and healthcare were usually free, and almost everyone had a job. But goods were often in short supply, and people had to queue for a long time. Freedom of opinion and freedom to travel were severely restricted.

Around 1989 to 1991 the communist governments in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union collapsed. Today communist parties still govern China, Vietnam, Laos and Cuba, and North Korea is also a one-party dictatorship. In 1916 and 1917 Lenin lived in exile in Zurich, on Spiegelgasse. In Switzerland the small **Party of Labour** has existed since 1944 and refers to communist ideas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A society without differences between rich and poor; the goal of communism.
The working men and women who own nothing except their labour power.
The state decides what is produced and how much.
A country in which only one single party is allowed to govern.

gewusst: The best-known sign of communism is the hammer and sickle, which stands for workers and peasants.
Karl Marx is buried in London, where he spent most of his life.

teile.einleitung: The flag of the Soviet Union was the red flag of the largest state in the world, which existed from 1922 to 1991. In the top left corner it showed a golden hammer and sickle with a star. It was one of the best-known symbols of communism.
wichtigste: The flag of the Soviet Union was red.
In the top left corner there was a hammer and sickle with a star, all in gold.
The red colour stood for the revolution and the workers' struggle.
The hammer and sickle stood for the alliance of workers and peasants.
The star was seen as a sign of the Communist Party.
The flag was introduced in 1923 and later only slightly changed.
On 25 December 1991 it was lowered from the Kremlin in Moscow for the last time.

abschnitte.text: The flag is completely **red** and twice as long as it is high. In the top left corner there is a crossed **hammer and sickle** in gold. Above it shines a **red star** with a golden border. The back of the flag was usually plain red, without any symbols.

The red colour recalls the **revolution** of 1917 and the blood spilled in the workers' struggle. The **hammer** stands for the workers in the factories, the **sickle** for the peasants in the fields. Together they show that both groups were supposed to lead the state jointly. The five-pointed star was seen as a symbol of the Communist Party; some also interpreted its points as the five continents.

The Soviet Union was founded at the end of **1922**, and the flag was introduced in 1923. Later the shape and size of the symbols were slightly adjusted a few times; the last version dates from 1980. Each of the **15 Soviet republics**, such as Ukraine or Kazakhstan, also had its own flag. Many of these were similarly red with a hammer and sickle, but with coloured stripes.

When the Soviet Union broke up at the end of 1991, the flag also lost its meaning. On the evening of **25 December 1991** Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as president. Shortly afterwards the red flag was lowered from the **Kremlin** in Moscow and replaced by the white, blue and red flag of Russia. The 15 republics became independent states with their own flags.

Today the flag of the Soviet Union is seen mainly in museums, films and history books. In some countries that suffered under Soviet rule, such as Lithuania or Ukraine, displaying such symbols in public is banned. For many people the flag is a reminder of oppression; for others it recalls the victory over Germany in the **Second World War**. That is why it is still a controversial symbol today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large communist state from 1922 to 1991, made up of Russia and 14 other republics.
The old fortress in Moscow where the government has its seat.
A sign that stands for a particular idea.
A state without a king; here, a member state of the Soviet Union.

gewusst: With more than 22 million square kilometres, the Soviet Union was the largest country on Earth by area.
Many people simply call the flag the red flag.
The flag of Vietnam also has a red background, but with a large yellow star in the middle.

teile.einleitung: The Cold War was the decades-long rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union after the Second World War. The two superpowers never fought each other directly, but they threatened each other with nuclear weapons. It lasted from about 1947 until the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991.
wichtigste: The Cold War was the political rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union without a direct war between them.
It lasted from about 1947 to 1991.
On one side were the USA and NATO, on the other the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact.
An Iron Curtain divided Europe into East and West.
Both sides built thousands of nuclear weapons.
In other parts of the world, such as Korea and Vietnam, there were real wars.
The Cold War ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991.

abschnitte.text: A war is called **cold** when the opponents are hostile to each other but do not shoot at each other directly with weapons. After the Second World War the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** faced each other as two superpowers. The USA stood for democracy and a market economy, the Soviet Union for communism. Both wanted to win over as many countries as possible to their side.

In 1946 the British politician Winston Churchill spoke of an **Iron Curtain** dividing Europe. In the West the USA and its allies founded **NATO** in 1949, and in the East the **Warsaw Pact** was formed in 1955. Germany was divided into two states, West Germany and the GDR. In 1961 the **Berlin Wall** was built, and it became the symbol of the Cold War.

Both sides built more and more **nuclear weapons**; at times they had more than 60,000 between them. Because a nuclear war would have destroyed both countries, neither dared to attack first. The most dangerous moment was the **Cuban Missile Crisis** in October 1962, when the Soviet Union stationed missiles in Cuba. In countries such as Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan there were so-called **proxy wars** in which many people died.

The superpowers also competed in space. In 1957 the Soviet Union sent the first satellite, **Sputnik 1**, into space, and in 1961 **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to fly into space. The USA responded with the Apollo programme. In 1969 the Americans Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon.

**Neutral Switzerland** did not belong to any alliance, but was close to the West economically and politically. Out of fear of a nuclear war, **shelters** were built in Switzerland for almost all inhabitants. Important conferences took place in **Geneva**; in 1985 US President Ronald Reagan and the Soviet party leader Mikhail Gorbachev met there. These talks helped to reduce tensions.

Under **Mikhail Gorbachev** the Soviet Union began reforms from 1985. In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell, and the communist governments in Eastern Europe collapsed. In 1990 Germany was reunified. In December **1991** the Soviet Union dissolved, and the Cold War was over.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state so strong that it has great influence all over the world.
The strictly guarded border that divided Europe into East and West.
When two opponents make more and more and stronger weapons to outdo each other.
A war in which two great powers do not fight each other themselves but support other countries or groups.
A defensive alliance of Western states, founded in 1949.

gewusst: After the Cuban Missile Crisis, a direct telephone and teleprinter link between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963, the so-called red telephone.
Switzerland still has so many shelters today that almost all its inhabitants would fit into them.
In 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other directly at Checkpoint Charlie in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: Karl Marx was a German philosopher, economist and journalist of the 19th century. He was a thinker with new ideas about a fair society and is regarded as the most important founder of communism. His books have strongly influenced world history, for good and for ill.
wichtigste: Karl Marx lived from 1818 to 1883.
He was born in Trier in Germany and died in London.
He was a thinker with new ideas about a fair society.
In 1848 he wrote the Communist Manifesto together with Friedrich Engels.
His main work is called Capital; the first volume appeared in 1867.
Marx criticised the fact that factory owners grew rich while workers stayed poor.
Later many parties and states referred to his ideas.

abschnitte.text: Karl Marx was born in **Trier** on 5 May **1818**; his father was a lawyer. He studied law and philosophy in Bonn and Berlin and received a doctorate in 1841. Instead of becoming a professor he became a journalist and ran the **Rheinische Zeitung** newspaper in Cologne. Because he criticised the government, the newspaper was banned in 1843.

Marx had to change countries several times and lived in Paris, Brussels and, from 1849, in **London**. There he lived with his wife **Jenny von Westphalen** and their children, often in great poverty. His friend **Friedrich Engels** supported the family with money. Almost every day Marx worked in the Reading Room of the British Museum.

In 1848 Marx and Engels published the **Communist Manifesto**, which ends with the call “Workers of all countries, unite!”. In 1867 the first volume of his main work, **Capital**, appeared. In it he examined how **capitalism** works. The further volumes were published by Engels after his death.

Marx observed that during industrialisation a few factory owners became very rich, while many workers worked long hours and earned little. He believed that history is shaped by the struggle between **classes**. In his view the workers would one day take power. The end result was to be a **classless society**, in which factories and land belong to everyone together.

Marx died in London on 14 March **1883** and is buried in Highgate Cemetery. His ideas influenced trade unions and social democratic parties, which campaigned for better working conditions. Communist states such as the Soviet Union or China also referred to him, but they became dictatorships that caused great suffering. His theories are still discussed and argued about at universities around the world today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who thinks about basic questions of life, thought and society.
An expert on the economy.
An economic system in which factories and companies belong to private people who want to make a profit with them.
Living abroad because you are persecuted in your home country.

gewusst: Marx lived in London from 1849 until his death, so more than 30 years in England.
His birthplace in Trier is now a museum that attracts many visitors from China.
Marx's handwriting was so hard to read that often only his wife and Engels could decipher it.

teile.einleitung: The Holodomor was a terrible famine in Ukraine in 1932 and 1933. It was partly caused by the Soviet government under Joseph Stalin, which took almost all the grain away from the peasants. Millions of people starved, even though Ukraine was known as the breadbasket of Europe.
wichtigste: The Holodomor was a famine in Ukraine in 1932 and 1933.
The Ukrainian word means roughly killing by hunger.
The famine was partly caused by the Soviet government under Stalin.
The state took grain and supplies from the peasants and did not let them flee to other areas.
Estimates put the number of deaths in Ukraine at about 3.5 to 5 million.
For decades it was forbidden to talk about it in the Soviet Union.
Ukraine and many other states today call the Holodomor a genocide.

abschnitte.text: The name **Holodomor** comes from Ukrainian and means roughly **killing by hunger**. It refers to the great famine in **Ukraine** in **1932 and 1933**. At that time Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union and had very fertile soil. Even so, millions of people died within a short time, above all peasant families in the countryside.

From 1929 the government forced the peasants to hand over their farms to **kolkhozes**, that is, large collective farms. Many peasants resisted, and the harvests got worse. Even so, the state demanded huge amounts of grain for the cities and for sale abroad. Anyone who could not deliver the required amount also had their supplies, livestock and other food taken away.

In August 1932 a law was passed that severely punished even the theft of a few **ears of grain** from a collective farm field. Villages that did not meet their quota were put on **blacklists** and were no longer allowed to buy goods. From January 1933 the starving peasants were not allowed to leave Ukraine to look for food elsewhere. There were also severe famines at that time in Kazakhstan and other parts of the Soviet Union.

The Soviet government denied that there was any famine at all. Help from abroad was refused, and foreign journalists were hardly allowed to visit the affected areas. In the Soviet Union it was **forbidden** for decades to talk about the Holodomor. Only in the late 1980s and after Ukraine became independent in 1991 was the subject openly researched.

In 2006 Ukraine declared the Holodomor by law to be a **genocide** against the Ukrainians. Many countries, for example Germany in 2022, have also recognised this, though experts still partly debate how it should be classified. Every year on the fourth Saturday in November, people in Ukraine remember the victims by putting candles in their windows. In the capital, **Kyiv**, there is a large Holodomor museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time when very many people do not have enough to eat and starve.
A large collective farm in the Soviet Union.
A crime aimed at destroying an entire ethnic group in whole or in part.
A day on which people remember an important or sad event.

gewusst: Because of its fertile black soil, Ukraine is often called the breadbasket of Europe.
In 1933 the Welsh journalist Gareth Jones was one of the first in the West to report on the famine.
On the day of remembrance, many families place ears of grain or bread beside the candle in memory of the victims.

teile.einleitung: Ho Chi Minh was a Vietnamese revolutionary and Vietnam's most important communist leader. For decades he fought for his country's independence from France, and he founded North Vietnam. In Vietnam he is still honoured today as Uncle Ho.
wichtigste: Ho Chi Minh lived from 1890 to 1969.
He was an important communist leader in Vietnam.
His birth name was Nguyen Sinh Cung; Ho Chi Minh is an alias.
As a young man he lived abroad for many years, including in France.
On 2 September 1945 he declared Vietnam's independence in Hanoi.
He led North Vietnam in the war against France and later against South Vietnam and the USA.
Vietnam's largest city, formerly Saigon, now bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Ho Chi Minh was born in central Vietnam in **1890**. At that time Vietnam belonged to France as part of **French Indochina**. His father was a scholar who rejected French rule. Even as a teenager Ho wanted Vietnam to be free and independent.

In 1911 he signed on as a kitchen hand on a ship and travelled around the world. He lived in London, in the USA and above all in **Paris**, where he worked as a photographer and cook. There he became a communist and in 1920 helped to found the French Communist Party. Later he lived in Moscow and China, and in 1930 he founded the **Indochinese Communist Party**.

In 1941 Ho returned to Vietnam and founded the **Viet Minh** movement. On 2 September **1945** he read out Vietnam's declaration of independence in **Hanoi**. But France did not want to give up the country, and the **Indochina War** broke out. In 1954 the Viet Minh won the Battle of Dien Bien Phu.

After the victory over France, many states met in 1954 at the **Geneva Conference on Indochina**. There it was decided to divide Vietnam provisionally into a north and a south. Ho Chi Minh became president of communist **North Vietnam**, which he ran as a one-party state. Opponents were persecuted, and many people died during a land reform.

Ho Chi Minh died in Hanoi on 2 September **1969**, in the middle of the Vietnam War. So he did not live to see the victory of the north in 1975. Although he had wanted to be cremated, his body was embalmed and now lies in the **Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum** in Hanoi. His picture appears on all Vietnamese banknotes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area ruled by a foreign state, usually one far away.
When a country governs itself and is not ruled by another state.
A large, splendid building that serves as a tomb.
A movement that fought for Vietnam's independence under Ho Chi Minh.

gewusst: Ho Chi Minh used more than 50 different names during his life.
The name Ho Chi Minh means roughly “he who enlightens”.
In Vietnam many people affectionately call him Bac Ho, which means Uncle Ho.

teile.einleitung: The Great Leap Forward was a campaign of the Chinese Communist Party under Mao Zedong from 1958 to about 1961. It was meant to turn China into a modern industrial country in the shortest possible time. However, the attempt failed and caused one of the worst famines in history.
wichtigste: The Great Leap Forward began in 1958 under Mao Zedong.
It was a failed attempt to industrialise China quickly.
At that time China wanted to overtake Great Britain in steel production.
Millions of people melted metal in small backyard furnaces, but it was mostly useless.
The peasants were grouped into huge people's communes.
From 1959 to 1961 the policy caused a devastating famine in which many millions died.
Afterwards Mao withdrew from day-to-day politics for a while.

abschnitte.text: After the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, the country was poor and lived mainly from agriculture. **Mao Zedong** wanted China to be able to keep up with the rich industrial countries within a few years. In 1958 he proclaimed the **Great Leap Forward**. One of the aims was to overtake Great Britain in steel production within 15 years.

All over the country people built small **backyard furnaces** out of clay and bricks. In them they melted down pots, tools and even door handles to make steel. But the metal was usually of such poor quality that it was hardly usable. Whole forests were cut down to heat the furnaces.

The farming villages were merged into huge **people's communes** with thousands of families. Private land and family kitchens were abolished, and everyone ate in communal canteens. New farming methods, such as sowing seeds very close together, were scientifically wrong and reduced the harvest. Because many peasants were working at the furnaces instead of in the fields, part of the harvest rotted.

Out of fear of punishment, local officials reported far too high harvest figures to Beijing. The state therefore took away so much grain that the peasants had hardly anything left to eat. From **1959 to 1961** there was a huge **famine**. Experts estimate the number of deaths at about 15 to 45 million people; exact figures are not known.

From 1961 the policy was stopped, and other politicians such as Liu Shaoqi and **Deng Xiaoping** tried to repair the economy. At first Mao lost influence, but in 1966 he took back power with the **Cultural Revolution**. In China public discussion of the famine is still restricted today. The Great Leap is seen as an example of how dangerous unrealistic plans and blind obedience can be.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from a farming country to a country with many factories and machines.
A huge grouping of villages in which land and work were organised collectively.
A time when very many people do not have enough to eat and starve.
A large, planned action to achieve a particular goal.

gewusst: During a campaign against sparrows, millions of birds were killed, after which harmful insects multiplied greatly.
At the same time as people were starving, China went on exporting grain abroad.
Some villages reported harvests that were ten times larger than in reality.

teile.einleitung: 1 May is Labour Day. On this day trade unions and employees in many countries demonstrate for fair wages and good working conditions. Its history begins with the struggle for shorter working days.
wichtigste: On 1 May 1886 many workers in the USA went on strike for the eight-hour day.
