During the Haymarket affair in Chicago on 4 May 1886, a bomb exploded and several people died.
In 1889 in Paris, the Second International declared 1 May a day of struggle for the workers' movement.
In 1890 1 May was marked with rallies in many countries for the first time, including Switzerland.
In Switzerland each canton decides for itself whether 1 May is a public holiday.
The red carnation and the colour red are symbols of May Day.

abschnitte.titel: The fight for the eight-hour day
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many people worked twelve hours or more a day in factories. The American workers' movement therefore demanded the **eight-hour day**: eight hours of work, eight hours of free time, eight hours of sleep. It called for a nationwide **strike** on 1 May 1886. A strike means that workers stop working together in order to get a demand met.

A few days after the strike, on 4 May 1886, a rally took place on the Haymarket in **Chicago**. A bomb exploded and several people died. Afterwards, leaders of the workers' movement were convicted and some were executed. Who threw the bomb was never found out. These events made 1 May a day of remembrance for the workers' movement.

In 1889 socialists from many countries met in Paris and founded the **Second International**, an alliance of workers' parties. They decided to demonstrate for the eight-hour day all over the world on 1 May. On 1 May 1890 workers took to the streets in many countries, including in Swiss cities. This became a yearly custom. In the USA itself, however, Labour Day is celebrated in September as “Labor Day”.

In Switzerland 1 May is **not a national public holiday**. The cantons decide for themselves. In Zurich it is treated like a Sunday, and it is also a day off in Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft. In many other cantons people work as normal. Even so, trade unions and parties hold marches and speeches in the larger cities every year.

Many participants wear a **red carnation** on their lapel on 1 May. Red is the traditional colour of the workers' movement. Flags, banners and speeches in public squares are typical. In Germany and Austria 1 May is a public holiday by law. In many areas there are also older spring customs, such as the maypole.

gewusst: Of all places, in the USA, where May Day began, it is not a holiday. “Labor Day” falls on the first Monday in September.
The demand “eight hours of work, eight hours of free time, eight hours of sleep” was a well-known slogan of the workers' movement.

teile.einleitung: Friedrich Engels was a German businessman, philosopher and writer of the 19th century. He was the closest friend and co-author of Karl Marx. Together they wrote the famous Communist Manifesto, which shaped the workers' movement all over the world.
wichtigste: Friedrich Engels lived from 1820 to 1895.
He was born in Barmen, which is now part of the city of Wuppertal.
He was the close friend and co-author of Karl Marx.
In 1848 the two of them published the Communist Manifesto.
Engels worked in his family's textile factory in Manchester in England.
With his money he supported Marx and his family for many years.
After Marx's death he published the last volumes of Marx's main work, Capital.

abschnitte.text: Friedrich Engels was born on 28 November **1820** in **Barmen**, today part of **Wuppertal**. His father owned a textile factory and was a devout, wealthy businessman. Friedrich was also meant to become a merchant and did an apprenticeship in the family business. On the side he was very interested in philosophy, politics and languages.

In 1842 Engels went to **Manchester**, at that time one of the most important industrial cities in the world. There he saw how hard the factory workers' lives were: long working days, dirty homes, child labour and disease. In 1845 he wrote about this in the book **The Condition of the Working Class in England**. It made him well known and also influenced Karl Marx.

In 1844 Engels and **Karl Marx** met in Paris and became close friends. In 1848 they wrote the **Communist Manifesto** together, which called on the workers of all countries to unite. During the revolution of 1848 and 1849 Engels fought in Baden and then fled via **Switzerland** to England. There he worked in the family business again and regularly sent Marx money.

When Marx died in 1883, Engels sorted out his notes. He published the second and third volumes of **Capital**, which Marx had not been able to finish. He also wrote books of his own, for example about the origin of the family and the state. He advised many socialist parties in Europe and was an important adviser to the workers' movement until his death.

Engels died in London on 5 August **1895**. As he had wished, his ashes were scattered in the sea off the English coast. His ideas influenced social democratic and communist parties. Later communist dictatorships also referred to him, even though he never lived to see these states himself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A public declaration in which a group sets out its aims.
The joining together of working men and women to fight for better wages and rights.
The period when machines and factories replaced work done by hand.
Someone who owns and runs a company.

gewusst: Engels was himself the son of a rich factory owner, yet he fought for workers' rights.
He spoke and read a great many languages, reportedly more than a dozen.
In Wuppertal a museum in the Engels House now recalls his life.

teile.einleitung: Erich Honecker was a German politician and for many years the most powerful man in the GDR. From 1971 to 1989 he led the ruling party, the SED, and with it the whole country. Under his rule the Berlin Wall was strictly guarded until it fell in the autumn of 1989.
wichtigste: Erich Honecker lived from 1912 to 1994.
For many years he was head of state of the GDR, that is, communist East Germany.
As a young communist he spent around ten years in prison during the Nazi period.
In 1961 he organised the building of the Berlin Wall.
In 1971 he replaced Walter Ulbricht as leader of the SED party.
In October 1989 he had to resign after huge protests.
He died in Chile in 1994.

abschnitte.text: Erich Honecker was born in 1912 in **Neunkirchen** in the Saarland. He trained as a roofer and joined the communist youth movement while still a teenager. After the Nazis came to power in 1933, he fought against them underground. In 1935 he was arrested and stayed in Brandenburg prison until the end of the war in **1945**.

After the war, in 1946, Honecker founded the **Free German Youth (FDJ)**, the youth organisation of the GDR. He rose higher and higher in the **SED** party. In August 1961 he directed the building of the **Berlin Wall**, which divided East and West Berlin. In 1971 he took over the leadership of the party from Walter Ulbricht, and from 1976 he also held the office of Chairman of the Council of State.

Honecker promised people more homes and better supplies, and indeed many prefabricated blocks of flats were built. At the same time there was often a shortage of goods such as tropical fruit or cars; people waited many years for a Trabant. The secret police, the **Stasi**, watched millions of people. Anyone who tried to leave the GDR without permission risked prison or death at the border.

In 1989 many GDR citizens fled to the West via Hungary, and in cities such as Leipzig hundreds of thousands demonstrated peacefully. Honecker did not want reforms like those in the Soviet Union under Mikhail Gorbachev. On **18 October 1989** he had to resign, and Egon Krenz became his successor. A few weeks later, on 9 November 1989, the Wall fell.

After the end of the GDR, Honecker fled to the Soviet Union, but in 1992 he was brought back to Germany. There he stood trial for the deaths at the Wall. Because he was seriously ill with cancer, the trial was stopped in 1993. He travelled to his wife Margot in **Chile**, where he died in May 1994.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German Democratic Republic, a communist state in East Germany from 1949 to 1990.
The Socialist Unity Party of Germany, which governed the GDR on its own.
The Ministry for State Security, the secret police of the GDR.

begriffe.wort: Chairman of the Council of State
begriffe.erklaerung: The office of head of state in the GDR.

gewusst: In 1987 Honecker became the first GDR head of state to make an official visit to West Germany, and he was received in Bonn.
His wife Margot Honecker was the GDR's education minister for more than 25 years.
As late as January 1989 Honecker said the Wall would still be standing in 50 and even 100 years.

teile.einleitung: The “hotline” was a direct communication link between the governments of the USA and the Soviet Union. It was set up in 1963 after the Cuban Missile Crisis so that the two superpowers could quickly reach an understanding in an emergency.
wichtigste: The hotline connected Washington and Moscow.
It was set up after the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
The agreement was signed in Geneva in June 1963.
The link went into operation on 30 August 1963.
At first it was not a telephone but a teleprinter.
It is often popularly called the “red telephone”.

abschnitte.text: In October 1962 the Soviet Union stationed **nuclear missiles** in Cuba, close to the USA. There was a threat of nuclear war. During the **Cuban Missile Crisis** it often took hours for messages to arrive between Washington and Moscow. Some first had to be translated and passed on through embassies. Both sides realised how dangerous such delays were.

Representatives of the USA and the Soviet Union signed the hotline agreement in **Geneva** in June 1963. During the **Cold War** the city was often a place for negotiations, because Switzerland is neutral. On **30 August 1963** the link went into operation. It ran through several countries in Europe.

At first the hotline was not a telephone at all. Written texts were sent with a **teleprinter**. This is a kind of typewriter that sends texts along a line. Written messages had one advantage: they could be translated carefully and precisely. This made misunderstandings easier to avoid.

To test it, an English sentence was sent: “The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog's back”. It is about a quick brown **fox** jumping over the back of a lazy **dog**. This sentence contains every letter of the English alphabet. That is why it was well suited for checking all the keys.

In films and in everyday speech people often talk about the “**red telephone**”. Red stands for danger and importance. The line was used to clear up **misunderstandings**, so that a nuclear war would not break out by mistake. Later the technology was renewed several times, for example with satellites.

gewusst: The test sentence with the fox and the dog is still often used today to check fonts and keyboards.
The link was tested regularly so that it would be sure to work in an emergency.

teile.einleitung: In the Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961, Cuban exiles with help from the USA tried to overthrow Fidel Castro's government in Cuba. The attack failed after about three days and became a serious defeat for the USA.
wichtigste: The landing began on 17 April 1961.
The CIA intelligence service planned the invasion and trained the Cuban exiles.
The unit was called Brigade 2506 and had about 1,400 men.
President John F. Kennedy gave the order.
The main fighting took place near Playa Girón.
At the end of 1962 the prisoners were released in exchange for food and medicine.

abschnitte.text: In 1959 **Fidel Castro** took power in Cuba after a revolution. He nationalised many companies, including American ones, and moved closer to the Soviet Union. Many Cubans fled to the USA. The US government wanted to overthrow Castro. The plan was drawn up by the **CIA** intelligence service while Eisenhower was still president.

The CIA trained around 1,400 Cuban exiles, **Brigade 2506**. Its name came from the service number of a member who had died in an accident during training. President **John F. Kennedy** gave the order in April 1961. On **17 April 1961** the invaders landed in the **Bay of Pigs** on the south coast of Cuba, at **Playa Girón** and Playa Larga. Officially, the involvement of the USA was supposed to stay hidden.

The Cuban army reacted quickly and was much stronger than expected. The hoped-for support from the population did not come. After about three days the invasion had failed. More than 1,100 invaders were taken prisoner. Kennedy publicly took responsibility for the failure. CIA director **Allen Dulles** had to leave his post at the end of 1961.

In December 1962 Cuba released the prisoners. In return it received **food and medicine** worth around 53 million dollars. In Cuba the event is still named after the beach of **Playa Girón** today and is celebrated as a victory.

On the eve of the fighting, Castro declared the Cuban revolution to be **socialist**. After that Cuba sought even more protection from the **Soviet Union**. In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles on the island, which led to the **Cuban Missile Crisis**. Because the USA and Cuba no longer had relations, from 1961 **Switzerland** represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as the protecting power.

gewusst: Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba for more than 50 years, until an American embassy was opened again in 2015.
In Spanish the Bay of Pigs is called “Bahía de Cochinos”.

teile.einleitung: The February Revolution of 1917 ended the rule of the tsars in Russia. Within a few days, protests against hunger and war turned into an overthrow, after which a Provisional Government took charge.
wichtigste: The revolution began in Petrograd, today's St Petersburg.
It is called the February Revolution because Russia still used the Julian calendar. By our calendar it was March.
On International Women's Day, women textile workers took to the streets.
The soldiers in the capital refused to shoot at the demonstrators.
Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, and Prince Georgy Lvov then led the Provisional Government.
From July 1917 Alexander Kerensky was head of government.

abschnitte.text: Russia had been fighting in the **First World War** since 1914 and had suffered heavy losses. In the winter of 1917 there was a shortage of food and fuel. Long queues formed outside the bakeries in **Petrograd**. The city had had this name since 1914 because the old name “Petersburg” sounded too German. Many people were exhausted and angry with the tsar's government.

Until 1918 Russia used the **Julian calendar**. At that time it was 13 days behind the **Gregorian calendar**, which we use today. So 23 February in the old style corresponds to 8 March. On that day, **International Women's Day**, women textile workers went on strike. Within a few days their protests turned into a **general strike**.

The tsar ordered the unrest to be crushed. But many regiments in Petrograd refused to shoot at the people and went over to the rebels. With that the government lost its power in the capital. Tsar **Nicholas II** abdicated in March 1917. The rule of the Romanov family, which had lasted more than 300 years, was over.

Politicians from the **Duma**, the parliament, formed a **Provisional Government**, that is, a temporary government. At first it was led by **Prince Georgy Lvov**, and from July 1917 by **Alexander Kerensky**. At the same time the **Petrograd Soviet** was formed, a council of workers and soldiers. With **Order No. 1** it placed the soldiers under elected committees. Because both sides held power, this is called dual power.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the October Revolution
abschnitte.text: The Provisional Government carried on the war against Germany. This made it unpopular with many soldiers and workers who were tired of war. In April 1917 **Lenin** returned from exile in Switzerland; he had most recently lived in Zurich. He demanded peace and “all power to the soviets”. In the **October Revolution** his Bolsheviks overthrew Kerensky's government.

gewusst: In 1917 Lenin travelled from Zurich by train right across Germany to Russia. The German government allowed the journey because it hoped the fighting in the east would end.
By our calendar, the October Revolution actually took place in November too.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Stalin was the dictator of the Soviet Union from the 1920s until his death in 1953. Under his rule the country became an industrial power and defeated Hitler's Germany in the Second World War. At the same time millions of people were persecuted, locked up in camps or killed.
wichtigste: Joseph Stalin lived from 1878 to 1953 and came from Georgia.
He was the dictator of the Soviet Union, under whom millions of people were persecuted.
His real name was Ioseb Jughashvili; Stalin means “the man of steel”.
After Lenin's death in 1924 he won the power struggle against his rivals.
With five-year plans and forced collectivisation he built up industry.
In the Great Terror from 1936 to 1938 he had hundreds of thousands executed.
In the Second World War he led the Soviet Union to victory over Germany.

abschnitte.text: Stalin was born in December **1878** in **Gori** in Georgia; his name was Ioseb Jughashvili. His mother wanted him to become a priest and sent him to a seminary in Tiflis. But there he became a revolutionary and joined Lenin's **Bolsheviks**. Because he took part in robberies and uprisings, he was arrested several times and exiled to Siberia.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917, Stalin rose in the party and in 1922 became its **general secretary**. After **Lenin's** death in 1924, several politicians fought for the leadership. Stalin got rid of his rivals, such as Leon Trotsky, one after another. By the end of the 1920s he was the undisputed sole ruler of the Soviet Union.

With the **five-year plans**, Stalin had huge factories, power stations and towns built in a short time. The peasants were forced to hand over their farms to **kolkhozes**. This led to severe famines, such as the Holodomor in Ukraine. Many building projects were carried out by prisoners from the **Gulag**.

Stalin distrusted everyone and had supposed enemies persecuted. In the **Great Terror** from 1936 to 1938 about 700,000 people were shot, including many officers and party members. In **show trials** the accused had to confess to crimes they had never committed. Whole ethnic groups, such as the Chechens or the Crimean Tatars, were deported to distant regions.

In 1939 Stalin signed a **non-aggression pact** with Hitler, but in 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union. After heavy losses the Red Army won victories, for example in the Battle of **Stalingrad**, and captured Berlin in 1945. Around 27 million people from the Soviet Union died in the war. After the war Stalin brought Eastern Europe under Soviet influence, and the Cold War began.

Stalin died on 5 March **1953** at his dacha near Moscow. During his lifetime he was worshipped like a hero and his pictures hung everywhere; this is called a **cult of personality**. In 1956 his successor Nikita Khrushchev criticised Stalin's crimes in a secret speech. Today historians see him as one of the cruellest dictators of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who governs alone and without control by a parliament or the courts.
When a ruler has to be worshipped excessively like a hero or demigod.
A trial in which the verdict has been decided in advance and which serves only as propaganda.
Forcibly moving people to another area.
The head of the Communist Party in the Soviet Union.

gewusst: From 1925 to 1961 the city of Volgograd was called Stalingrad.
In photos from Stalin's time, people who had fallen out of favour were often retouched out afterwards.
In Gori, Stalin's birthplace, there is still a large Stalin Museum today.

teile.einleitung: According to Karl Marx, the classless society is the final goal of the communist movement. It means a society without rich and poor, in which factories, land and machines belong to everyone together. This goal has never been reached in any country in the world.
wichtigste: According to Karl Marx, the classless society was the long-term final goal of the communist movement.
In it there was to be no more private ownership of the means of production.
According to Marx, without owners and people who own nothing there would also be no classes and no class struggle.
The way there was to lead through a revolution and a transition period.
In the end even the state was to become unnecessary and wither away.
No communist country has ever reached this goal.
Instead a new, privileged ruling class often formed in these states.

abschnitte.text: A **classless society** is a society in which there are no longer classes such as workers and factory owners. Factories, machines and land, the so-called **means of production**, are to belong to everyone together. But you may still own personal things such as clothes, furniture or books. Nobody should have to work for someone else any more so that the other person becomes rich.

Marx imagined the path in several stages. First the workers were to take power in a **revolution**. In a transition period, which he called the **dictatorship of the proletariat**, the working class was to run the state. This was to be followed by **socialism** and finally by communism as a classless society.

abschnitte.titel: What it was meant to look like
abschnitte.text: In communism the rule was to be: from each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs. This means everyone works as well as they can and gets what they need. Because there would be no more classes fighting each other, the **state** with its police and army would also no longer be needed. Engels said that the state would then **wither away**.

In states such as the Soviet Union, China or the GDR, private ownership of factories and land was abolished. But instead of disappearing, the state became more and more powerful and controlled the whole of life. A new upper class of party officials emerged, known as the **nomenklatura**. In 1957 the Yugoslav politician Milovan Djilas described this group in his book The New Class.

abschnitte.titel: Similar ideas on a small scale
abschnitte.text: The idea of a community without rich and poor is much older than Marx; as early as 1516 the Englishman Thomas More described the imaginary island of **Utopia**. In Israel there are the **kibbutzim**, villages in which for a long time the inhabitants owned everything together and lived together voluntarily. **Cooperatives**, such as the housing cooperatives in Switzerland, also belong jointly to many members. But they are part of a market economy and not a classless society.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of people in a similar economic situation, for example the working class.
Something that belongs to a single person or company.
The idea of an ideal society that does not yet exist in reality.
The privileged ruling class in communist states.
An association of people who jointly own a business.

gewusst: The word Utopia was invented by Thomas More and means something like “no place”.
Switzerland's two largest retailers, Migros and Coop, are organised as cooperatives.
Marx himself never described exactly what everyday life in a classless society would be like.

teile.einleitung: Kim Jong-un is the ruler of North Korea, one of the most isolated countries in the world. He has ruled the communist country since the end of 2011 as the successor to his father and grandfather. He is known around the world mainly because of his country's nuclear weapons and missile tests.
wichtigste: Kim Jong-un rules communist North Korea today.
He came to power at the end of 2011 after the death of his father Kim Jong-il.
His grandfather Kim Il-sung founded North Korea in 1948.
As a teenager he went to school near Bern under a different name.
Under him North Korea has tested several atomic bombs and many missiles.
In 2018 and 2019 he met US President Donald Trump several times.
In North Korea there are no free elections, no free press and prison camps for opponents.

abschnitte.text: Kim Jong-un was born in the 1980s; the exact year is not known for certain, and **1984** is usually given. He is a son of **Kim Jong-il**, who ruled North Korea from 1994 to 2011. As a teenager he lived for some years in **Switzerland** and went to a school in Liebefeld near Bern under a false name. After that he studied at a military university in Pyongyang.

North Korea has been ruled by the same family since it was founded in **1948**. First **Kim Il-sung** ruled, then his son Kim Jong-il, and since December **2011** his son Kim Jong-un. The Kim family is worshipped like heroes in North Korea, and their pictures hang everywhere. Kim Jong-un is head of the ruling **Workers' Party of Korea** and head of state.

Under Kim Jong-un North Korea has greatly expanded its **nuclear weapons** and carried out several underground nuclear tests, the last in 2017. The country also repeatedly tests missiles that can fly very long distances. The United Nations has therefore imposed strict **sanctions** on North Korea. Neighbouring countries such as South Korea and Japan feel threatened by this.

In 2018 Kim Jong-un became the first North Korean ruler to meet a sitting US president, **Donald Trump**, in Singapore. This was followed in 2019 by a meeting in Hanoi and a short meeting at the border in **Panmunjom**. He also met the South Korean president several times. But no lasting agreement on nuclear weapons was reached.

North Korea is a strict **dictatorship** and almost completely cut off from the world. People may not travel freely, and the internet is blocked for almost everyone. Critics of the government are sent to **prison camps**, and even high-ranking people have been executed, such as Kim's uncle in 2013. Many people are poor, and there have been repeated famines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who holds power in a state, often without having been elected.
Penalties against a country, for example a ban on trade.
A form of rule in which one person or group has all the power and the people cannot vote freely.
The capital of North Korea.

gewusst: Kim Jong-un is said to have been a big basketball fan during his school days in Switzerland.
North Korea has its own calendar, which begins with the year Kim Il-sung was born.
When he came to power, Kim Jong-un was only about 27 years old.

teile.einleitung: The Soviet Union was founded on 30 December 1922. It was a union of Soviet republics led by the Communist Party and lasted until 1991.
wichtigste: The founding treaty was signed in Moscow on 30 December 1922.
The full name was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, USSR for short.
Four republics founded the state: Russia, Ukraine, Belorussia and Transcaucasia.
In 1924 the Soviet Union received its first constitution.
The flag was red and showed a hammer, a sickle and a star.
Until 1944 the Internationale was the anthem of the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: In 1917 the Bolsheviks under **Lenin** had taken power in Russia. This was followed by a long civil war, which they won. Soviet republics were also set up in other areas of the former Russian Empire. On **30 December 1922** their representatives signed the founding treaty in **Moscow**. This created the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics**, **USSR** for short. In Russian the abbreviation was SSSR.

The Soviet Union was founded by four republics: **Russia**, **Ukraine**, **Belorussia** and the **Transcaucasian Republic**. The last of these united Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan and lasted until 1936. After that the three countries became separate Union republics. Already in 1922 there was a dispute over Georgia, the so-called **Georgian Affair**. Stalin acted harshly against Georgian communists, which Lenin sharply criticised.

At the beginning of **1924** the USSR received its first **constitution**. Later constitutions followed in 1936 and 1977. The **flag** was red and showed a **hammer and sickle** in the top left corner with a star above. The hammer and sickle stood for the workers and the peasants. Until 1944 the anthem was the **Internationale**, the battle song of the workers' movement from France.

For a long time Switzerland had **no diplomatic relations** with the Soviet Union. In 1923 the Soviet diplomat **Vatslav Vorovsky** was shot dead in Lausanne. A Swiss court acquitted the killer, which greatly angered the Soviet Union. Only in 1946 did the two countries establish diplomatic relations.

Over time more republics were added, for example in Central Asia. The **Baltic states** were occupied and annexed in 1940. In the end the Soviet Union consisted of 15 Union republics. It was the largest state on Earth by area. In 1991 it broke up into independent states.

gewusst: Lenin barely lived to see the first constitution; he died in January 1924.
The Soviet Union stretched across eleven time zones, from Europe to the Pacific.

teile.einleitung: Glasnost is a Russian word meaning “openness”. That was the name Mikhail Gorbachev gave to his policy of relaxing censorship in the Soviet Union from 1985. Together with perestroika, it changed the country greatly.
wichtigste: Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the CPSU in March 1985.
Glasnost means openness, perestroika means restructuring.
Newspapers were increasingly allowed to criticise problems openly.
The Chernobyl disaster in 1986 gave glasnost new momentum.
Banned books such as “Doctor Zhivago” were allowed to be published.
In 1990 Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: In the Soviet Union the Communist Party decided what appeared in newspapers, books and on television. Criticising the government was dangerous. The economy was hardly making progress. In March 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary of the **CPSU**, that is, head of the party. He wanted to renew the rigid system and relied on **glasnost**, on openness, to do so.

Alongside glasnost there was **perestroika**. The word means “restructuring” or “reshaping”. Perestroika was meant to modernise the **planned economy**, that is, the economy run by the state. Glasnost was meant to make sure that problems were discussed openly. Gorbachev believed that mistakes can only be fixed if people talk about them.

In April 1986 the **Chernobyl reactor accident** happened in Ukraine. At first the authorities kept quiet about the disaster for days, even though radioactive clouds drifted as far as Western Europe. Increased radiation was measured in Switzerland too. Gorbachev concluded that more openness was needed. After that, glasnost gained momentum.

With glasnost, **censorship** was relaxed. The media reported on corruption, environmental problems and government mistakes. People were allowed to speak openly about the **crimes under Stalin**, when millions of people were persecuted. At the end of 1986 the civil rights campaigner **Andrei Sakharov** was allowed to return to Moscow from exile in Gorky. In 1988 Boris Pasternak's long-banned novel “**Doctor Zhivago**” was published in the Soviet Union too.

In March 1990 **Article 6** of the constitution, which had laid down the leading role of the party, was changed. This made other parties possible. In the same year Gorbachev received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for his part in the peaceful end of the Cold War. But the new openness also strengthened independence movements in many republics. At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union broke up.

gewusst: In the 1980s the words “glasnost” and “perestroika” became widely known in Switzerland and the rest of the West too.
Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958, but he had to turn it down under pressure from the government.

teile.einleitung: The First International was an alliance of workers' organisations from many countries. It was founded in London in 1864 and its official name was the International Workingmen's Association. Switzerland played an important part in its history.
wichtigste: The First International was founded in London in 1864.
In 1869 its congress met in Basel.
In 1868 Bakunin founded the Alliance of Socialist Democracy in Geneva.
In 1872 Bakunin and James Guillaume were expelled.
In the same year the anti-authoritarian International was founded in Saint-Imier.
In 1876 the First International was dissolved in Philadelphia.

abschnitte.text: In 1864 representatives of workers' organisations from several countries met in **London**. They founded the **International Workingmen's Association**, later called the **First International**. The aim was for working people to support each other across national borders. **Karl Marx** belonged to the leading **General Council** and shaped the organisation strongly. Several congresses took place in Switzerland, for example in Geneva, Lausanne and Basel.

In **Geneva** the German revolutionary **Johann Philipp Becker** organised the German-speaking sections. He had taken part in uprisings in 1848 and 1849 and published the magazine “Der Vorbote” (The Herald). In 1869 the congress met in **Basel**. There people argued about abolishing the right of inheritance, and the conflict between Marx and Bakunin came clearly into the open.

In 1868 the Russian anarchist **Mikhail Bakunin** founded the **Alliance of Socialist Democracy** in Geneva. He rejected every kind of state, even a workers' state. The General Council around Marx saw the Alliance as an attempt to take over the International from within. Bakunin found support in the **Jura Federation**, an association of watchmakers in the Swiss Jura. Its leading figure was the Neuchâtel teacher **James Guillaume**.

At the **Hague Congress** in 1872, Bakunin and Guillaume were expelled. The General Council was moved to **New York** to keep it away from the influence of Bakunin's followers. In September 1872 these followers founded the **anti-authoritarian International** in **Saint-Imier** in the Bernese Jura. The First International quickly lost importance. In 1876 a conference in **Philadelphia** decided to dissolve it.

gewusst: The Congress of Saint-Imier is seen as the birth of the anarchist movement.
The watchmakers in the Jura often worked in small workshops and valued running their own affairs.

thx0pov.t: Founding of the People's Republic of China

teile.einleitung: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Before that, the communists had won the civil war against the Kuomintang. Today the day is China's national holiday.
wichtigste: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949 from the Gate of Heavenly Peace.
The Kuomintang government under Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan.
Beijing became the capital again; before that, the Kuomintang had governed from Nanjing.
Zhou Enlai became the first premier.
The Common Programme served as a provisional constitution.
In 1950 China signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: For decades two parties fought for power in China: the **Communist Party** under **Mao Zedong** and the nationalist **Kuomintang** under **Chiang Kai-shek**. After the Second World War the **civil war** flared up again. In 1949 the communists won. Chiang Kai-shek withdrew with his government and army to the island of **Taiwan**, where the Republic of China still exists today.

In September 1949 the **Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference** met. It brought together communists, smaller parties and organisations. It elected the government and decided on the flag, the anthem and the capital. Around this time Mao spoke the famous sentence: “The Chinese people have stood up.” On **1 October 1949** he proclaimed the People's Republic from the **Gate of Heavenly Peace** on Tiananmen Square.

**Beijing** became the capital again; the Kuomintang had previously governed from Nanjing. The first **premier** was **Zhou Enlai**, who led the government until his death in 1976. The **Common Programme**, adopted in September 1949, served as a provisional constitution. A proper constitution followed in 1954.

The flag of the People's Republic is red and shows five yellow stars. The **large star** stands for leadership by the Communist Party. The four small stars stand for the social classes of the people. They all point towards the large star.

In February 1950 Mao and **Stalin** signed a treaty of friendship and alliance in Moscow. The Soviet Union then helped China with loans and experts. At first many Western countries recognised only the government in Taiwan. But **Switzerland** was one of the first Western states to recognise the People's Republic, in January 1950.

gewusst: On 1 October the “Golden Week” begins in China, a holiday week in which millions of people travel.
A large portrait of Mao still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace today.

teile.einleitung: The Communist International, Comintern for short, was a worldwide alliance of communist parties. It was founded in Moscow in 1919 and dissolved again in 1943. Its leadership was firmly in the hands of the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The Comintern was founded in Moscow in 1919.
It is also called the Third International.
From 1920 parties had to meet 21 conditions to be admitted.
The Executive Committee in Moscow gave the parties binding instructions.
In 1935 it decided on the Popular Front against fascism.
Georgi Dimitrov was general secretary from 1935 to 1943.
Stalin dissolved the Comintern in 1943.

abschnitte.text: The Comintern was founded in **Moscow** in **March 1919** on **Lenin's** initiative. Its aim was **world revolution**. It is also called the **Third International**. It saw itself as the successor to Marx's First International and as the counterpart to the social democrats' **Second International**. The Communist Party of Switzerland also became a member.

In **1920** the second world congress adopted the **21 conditions of admission**. Anyone who wanted to become a member had to accept strict discipline and break with moderate socialists. Between the world congresses the organisation was led by the **Executive Committee**, **ECCI** for short. It sat in Moscow and gave binding instructions to the parties in the individual countries.

Around **1929** the Comintern fought the social democrats with the slogan **“social fascism”**. In this way it put them on the same level as the fascists. This attitude made joint resistance against Nazism harder in Germany. After Hitler seized power the course changed: in **1935** the seventh world congress decided on the **Popular Front** against fascism. Popular Front governments were formed in France and Spain.

From 1935 to 1943 the Bulgarian **Georgi Dimitrov** was general secretary. He had become well known in 1933 at the **Reichstag fire trial** in Leipzig, because he defended himself skilfully and was acquitted. In **May 1943** **Stalin** dissolved the Comintern. During the Second World War he wanted to reassure his Western allies in this way.

gewusst: The word “Comintern” is an abbreviation from Russian for Communist International.
After the Reichstag fire trial, Georgi Dimitrov lived in Moscow and led the Comintern from there.

teile.einleitung: The Secret Speech was given by the Soviet party leader Nikita Khrushchev in February 1956. In it he openly criticised the crimes of his predecessor Joseph Stalin for the first time. The speech changed the communist world.
wichtigste: Khrushchev gave the speech on 25 February 1956 at the 20th Congress of the CPSU.
It was titled “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences”.
The speech lasted about four hours and took place in a closed session.
Khrushchev quoted Lenin's Testament to incriminate Stalin.
The text reached the West through a copy from Poland.
In the Soviet Union the speech was not officially published until 1989.

abschnitte.titel: The speech at the party congress
abschnitte.text: Stalin had died in 1953. **Nikita Khrushchev** then became First Secretary of the Communist Party. At the **20th Congress of the CPSU**, on 25 February 1956, he spoke in a **closed session** after the official end of the congress. Only Soviet delegates were admitted, not even foreign communist parties. He spoke for about four hours.

abschnitte.titel: Criticism of the cult of personality
abschnitte.text: The speech was called “**On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences**”. A **cult of personality** means that a leader is worshipped almost like a god. Khrushchev accused Stalin of letting himself be worshipped in this way. He spoke about **mass arrests**, torture and the execution of loyal party members. He kept quiet about his own part in these purges. Many delegates were shocked.

To incriminate Stalin, Khrushchev read from **Lenin's Testament**. In this letter from 1922 and 1923 Lenin had called Stalin too rude. He had suggested removing him as general secretary. This text had been kept secret for a long time. Now the delegates heard it for the first time.

The speech was supposed to stay secret. But in **Poland** a copy got into the hands of a journalist and from there to the Israeli secret service. In June 1956 the “New York Times” published the text. In the Soviet Union itself the speech was not officially printed until 1989, under **Gorbachev**.

The criticism of Stalin began **de-Stalinisation**. Many political prisoners were released, and Stalin's picture gradually disappeared from public life. In the Eastern Bloc the speech raised hopes of more freedom. In **Hungary** a popular uprising broke out in the autumn of 1956, which Soviet tanks crushed in November.

gewusst: Although the speech was called “secret”, it was soon read out at party meetings in the Soviet Union.
In 1961 Stalin's body was removed from the mausoleum on Red Square, where it had lain beside Lenin.

teile.einleitung: The Juche ideology is the official state ideology of North Korea. The word means roughly “self-reliance”. According to this doctrine, the country should provide for itself and follow the leader.
wichtigste: Juche means roughly self-reliance or independence.
It is laid down in North Korea's constitution.
Kim Il-sung is regarded as its founder.
The Juche Tower in Pyongyang is about 170 metres high.
The Juche calendar begins with the year Kim Il-sung was born, 1912.
From the 1990s the Songun policy put the military first.

abschnitte.text: In Korean **Juche** means roughly “**self-reliance**”. According to this idea, a country should **provide for itself** politically, economically and militarily and not depend on anyone. The Juche ideology is North Korea's official **state ideology** and is written into the constitution. It shapes politics, schools and art there.

**Kim Il-sung**, North Korea's first ruler, is regarded as its founder. He put the Juche idea in the foreground from the 1950s. According to the doctrine, the people need a great **leader** to guide them. In this way the ideology justifies the power of the **Kim family**, which has ruled the country since it was founded. His successors developed the doctrine further.

In the capital, **Pyongyang**, stands the **Juche Tower**. It was inaugurated in 1982 for Kim Il-sung's 70th birthday and, with the flame at the top, is about 170 metres high. Since 1997 there has also been the **Juche calendar**. It begins with the year 1912, when Kim Il-sung was born.

North Korea trades very little with other countries and has hardly any contact with the outside world. The country has stayed poor and isolated. In the 1990s it suffered a severe **famine**. During this time the **Songun** policy also emerged, which means “military first”. The army was given priority for money and resources.

gewusst: In the Juche calendar 1912 is year 1, so 2012 is year 101.
The Juche Tower is slightly taller than the Washington Monument in the USA.

teile.einleitung: The Berlin Wall Memorial is on Bernauer Strasse in Berlin. It recalls the division of the city from 1961 to 1989 and the people who lost their lives at the Wall.
wichtigste: The memorial is on Bernauer Strasse.
A section of the Wall with the border strip and a watchtower has been preserved there.
In the “Window of Remembrance”, photos commemorate the people who died at the Wall.
From a viewing platform you can look down on the old border strip.
In Berlin a double row of cobblestones shows where the Wall stood.

abschnitte.text: From 1961 to 1989 the **Berlin Wall** separated the eastern part of the city from the western part. On **Bernauer Strasse** the border ran right along the houses. When the Wall was built, people jumped out of windows here to get to the West. Today a section of the border installations, with the **death strip** and a **watchtower**, has been preserved at this spot. So you can see what the border really looked like.

The memorial especially remembers the people who died at the Wall, mostly while trying to escape. In the **Window of Remembrance** there is a photo with a name for many of them. The **Chapel of Reconciliation** also stands on the site. It was built where a church in the border strip used to stand; that church was blown up in 1985.

From a **viewing platform** you look down on the preserved section of the border installations. You can see how wide the border strip was and how hard it was to get across. Throughout the city, a **double row of cobblestones** in the ground also shows the course of the Wall. This lets you follow it even where nothing of it is left standing.

gewusst: Escape helpers dug several tunnels under Bernauer Strasse, through which people fled to the West.

teile.einleitung: Collectivisation means that many small farms are merged into large collective or state-run enterprises. In communist countries such as the Soviet Union, China or the GDR, this was often carried out by force. The consequences were terrible for millions of people.
wichtigste: In collectivisation, farms were merged into large state or collective farms.
In the process the farmers usually lost their own land and livestock.
In the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin forced through collectivisation from 1929.
There the large farms were called kolkhozes and sovkhozes.
In Ukraine and other areas millions of people died in a famine in 1932 and 1933.
In China huge people's communes were set up from 1958.
In the GDR there were the Agricultural Production Cooperatives, LPG for short.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “collectivus”, meaning “gathered together”. Instead of many separate family farms, there were to be a few **large enterprises**. The land, the machines and often the animals then belonged to the community or the state. The communists believed that large farms would produce more food and that there would no longer be any rich big farmers.

From 1929 Stalin forced the farmers in the Soviet Union to bring their farms into **kolkhozes**. A kolkhoz was a collective farm, whereas a **sovkhoz** was a purely state-owned farm. Anyone who resisted was often persecuted as a “kulak”, that is, a rich farmer. Hundreds of thousands of families had their property taken away and were deported to distant regions such as Siberia.

The forced change threw agriculture into chaos. Many farmers preferred to slaughter their livestock rather than hand it over. At the same time the state demanded large amounts of grain. As a result there was a severe famine in 1932 and 1933, especially in Ukraine, where it is called the **Holodomor**.

In China, from 1958, Mao Zedong introduced the **people's communes** as part of the so-called “Great Leap Forward”. In them, often thousands of families lived and worked together. The plans were unrealistic, and the harvests were wrongly reported. In the famine that followed, from 1959 to 1961, many millions of people died.

In the GDR the farmers were grouped together in **LPGs** in the 1950s, almost completely by 1960. After the end of communism, around 1989 to 1991, many of these enterprises were dissolved or converted. Some former LPGs still exist today as large agricultural businesses. In Switzerland farmers also work together in cooperatives, but they do so voluntarily and their land remains their own property.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large farm in the Soviet Union that belonged jointly to its members but was controlled by the state.
A farm in the Soviet Union that belonged directly to the state.
An insulting term for farmers who were thought to be rich and were persecuted for that reason.
A huge community in China in which thousands of families worked and lived together.
When someone's property is taken away from them.

gewusst: In some people's communes in China, people ate in large communal canteens instead of at home.
Even in the Soviet Union, kolkhoz farmers were allowed to farm a small garden plot of their own, which often produced especially high yields.

teile.einleitung: Common property means things that do not belong to a single person but to a whole group together. The idea is very old. In Switzerland it is known, for example, from the Allmend and from cooperatives.
wichtigste: Common property belongs to everyone in a group together; private property belongs to a single person.
The word “communism” comes from the Latin “communis”, which means “shared” or “common”.
An Allmend is land that the people of a village use together.
A cooperative is a business that belongs jointly to its members.
Marx and Engels wanted to abolish the private ownership of factories.
In the Soviet Union the state controlled factories and land.

abschnitte.text: **Private property** belongs to a single person or family, and they alone may decide about it. **Common property**, on the other hand, belongs to everyone in a group together. Everyone may use it, but everyone is also responsible for it. The word **communism** comes from the Latin “communis”, meaning “shared”. In communism, many things are meant to belong to everyone together.

Switzerland has had the **Allmend** since the Middle Ages. These are meadows, pastures or forests that the people of a village use together. In the past, farmers drove their cattle together onto the common pasture. In many municipalities such land is still managed today by **corporations**. Alpine pastures are also often used jointly.

A **cooperative** is a business that belongs jointly to its members. Usually each member has one vote, no matter how much money they have put in. In Switzerland many housing cooperatives and farming businesses are organised in this way. The big retailers **Migros** and **Coop** are also cooperatives.

**Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** wanted no one to own a factory on their own any more. Private ownership of factories and machines was to be abolished. In the **Soviet Union** factories and farms were handed over to the **state**, which then made the decisions about them. Many farming families had to give up their fields and work in large collective farms, the **kolkhozes**.

The first **kibbutzim** were founded in Israel at the beginning of the 20th century. In a **kibbutz** people lived and worked together and shared their possessions. In the past almost everything there belonged to everyone together, even clothes. Today many kibbutzim are organised less strictly, and members have more property of their own.

gewusst: The Allmend in Bern and the Allmend in Zurich still recall the old common land in their names.
A member of a cooperative is called a cooperative member, in German “Genossenschafter” or “Genossenschafterin”.

teile.einleitung: The Gulag was a huge system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union. Millions of people had to do forced labour there in terrible conditions, often in freezing cold in Siberia. Many of them had committed no crime but were simply seen as opponents of the government.
wichtigste: The Gulag was a system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union.
The word is a Russian abbreviation for Main Administration of Camps.
The Gulag was at its worst under Joseph Stalin, from the 1930s to the early 1950s.
Millions of prisoners had to build canals, railway lines and mines.
Many camps were in very cold, remote areas such as Siberia or Kolyma.
Hunger, cold and hard work led to the deaths of a great many prisoners.
The writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn made the Gulag known around the world.

abschnitte.text: The word **Gulag** is an abbreviation from Russian and means **Main Administration of Camps**. From 1930 this authority ran hundreds of camps throughout the Soviet Union. There were already camps soon after the revolution, for example from 1923 on the **Solovetsky Islands** in the White Sea. Today the word Gulag is used generally for the whole camp system.

abschnitte.titel: Who was sent to the Gulag?
abschnitte.text: It was not only criminals who were sent to the camps, but also a great many **political prisoners**. Even a joke about Stalin, a visit abroad or a false accusation by neighbours could be enough. Peasants who resisted collectivisation and whole ethnic groups were also deported. Experts estimate that altogether around 18 million people passed through the camps.

abschnitte.titel: Life and work in the camps
abschnitte.text: The prisoners had to do **forced labour**, for example felling trees, mining gold or building railway lines. One well-known project was the **White Sea-Baltic Canal**, which was dug almost entirely with shovels and wheelbarrows. The camps were often in freezing regions such as **Kolyma** or Vorkuta, where it could reach minus 40 degrees in winter. There was too little food and warm clothing, so more than a million people died there.

After Stalin's death in March **1953**, many prisoners were released in an amnesty. In 1956 the new party leader Nikita Khrushchev criticised Stalin's crimes. After that the large camp system was reduced, and the Gulag authority was dissolved in 1960. But there were still political prisoners in the Soviet Union until the 1980s.

The writer **Alexander Solzhenitsyn** spent eight years in the camps himself and described everyday life there in his books. His work **The Gulag Archipelago** was published in the West in 1973 and made the camps known all over the world. For decades the Russian organisation **Memorial** collected the names and stories of the victims. It was banned in Russia in 2021 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work that people have to do against their will and without fair pay.
A person who is locked up because they think differently from the government.
When the state cancels the sentences of many prisoners at once.
A group of islands; Solzhenitsyn compared the many camps to islands.

gewusst: Alexander Solzhenitsyn received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970.
The road through the Kolyma region is often called the Road of Bones, because many prisoners died building it.
After he was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1974, Solzhenitsyn first lived in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: FRELIMO is a party in Mozambique in south-east Africa. It began as a liberation movement against Portuguese colonial rule and has governed the country since independence in 1975.
wichtigste: FRELIMO was founded in 1962 in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.
Its first president was Eduardo Mondlane, who was killed by a parcel bomb in 1969.
On 25 June 1975 Mozambique became independent, and Samora Machel became its first president.
From 1977 to 1992 there was a civil war between the FRELIMO government and RENAMO.
The peace treaty was signed in Rome in 1992.
In 1989 FRELIMO gave up Marxism-Leninism.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Mozambique was a **colony** of Portugal, which means the country was ruled by Portugal. In 1962 several groups in neighbouring Tanzania joined together to form **FRELIMO**. The name is an abbreviation of “Mozambique Liberation Front” in Portuguese. It was founded in **Dar es Salaam**. From 1964 FRELIMO waged an armed struggle against the colonial power.

The first president of FRELIMO was **Eduardo Mondlane**. He had been taught at schools of the **Swiss Mission** in Mozambique and later studied in the USA. Mondlane led the movement until 1969. In February 1969 he died in Dar es Salaam when a parcel bomb hidden in a book exploded. Those responsible were never clearly identified.

In 1974 the **Carnation Revolution** in Portugal overthrew the dictatorship. The new government wanted to release the colonies. On **25 June 1975** Mozambique became independent, and **Samora Machel** became its first president. FRELIMO became the state party and organised the country according to **Marxism-Leninism**, that is, the doctrine of the Soviet Union. At first other parties were not allowed.

From 1977 the government fought against the rebel movement **RENAMO**. It was supported first by Rhodesia and later by South Africa. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and destroyed many villages. In 1986 Samora Machel died in a plane crash in South Africa; the cause is still disputed today. In October 1992 the peace treaty was signed in **Rome**, brokered mainly by the Catholic Community of Sant'Egidio.

In 1989 FRELIMO gave up Marxism-Leninism as its guiding principle. In 1990 Mozambique got a new constitution with a **multi-party system**. In 1994 the first free elections took place, and FRELIMO won them. Since then it has formed the government, and RENAMO is the largest opposition party.

gewusst: The Swiss Mission, at whose schools Mondlane studied, was a missionary society from French-speaking Switzerland.
Independence Day on 25 June is a national holiday in Mozambique.

teile.einleitung: The Hitler-Stalin Pact was a treaty between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. It was signed on 23 August 1939, a few days before the start of the Second World War. In a secret addition the two dictatorships divided Eastern Europe between them.
wichtigste: The pact was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939.
It was signed by the foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov.
Officially it was a non-aggression pact.
In the secret additional protocol, Eastern Europe was divided into spheres of interest.
In September 1939 first Germany and then the Soviet Union attacked Poland.
With Operation Barbarossa, Hitler broke the pact on 22 June 1941.

abschnitte.text: Nazis and communists were bitter enemies. So the world was all the more surprised when a treaty between the two states was signed in Moscow on **23 August 1939**. Foreign Minister **Joachim von Ribbentrop** signed for Germany and **Vyacheslav Molotov** for the Soviet Union. That is why the treaty is also called the **Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact**. Officially it was a **non-aggression pact**: both promised not to attack each other.

The treaty included a **secret additional protocol**. In it Germany and the Soviet Union divided Eastern Europe into **spheres of interest**. In the Boundary and Friendship Treaty of September 1939, **Lithuania** was assigned to the Soviet side, and in return Germany received Polish territory. The Soviet Union denied that the protocol existed until 1989.

On **1 September 1939** Germany attacked **Poland**, and this started the Second World War. On 17 September the Red Army marched in from the east. Poland was divided between the two states. In 1940 the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, killed thousands of Polish prisoners, many of them in the forest of **Katyn**. The Soviet Union only admitted this crime in 1990.

The Baltic states of **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania** had been assigned to the Soviet Union. In 1940 they were occupied and incorporated as Soviet republics. The pact also included an **economic agreement**. The Soviet Union supplied raw materials such as oil and grain and in return received machines and industrial goods.

On **22 June 1941** the German armed forces attacked the Soviet Union without a declaration of war. This attack was called **Operation Barbarossa**. Stalin had not taken warnings about it seriously. With that the pact was broken, and from then on the Soviet Union fought on the side of the Allies against Germany.

gewusst: On 23 August 1989, exactly 50 years after the pact, around two million people formed a human chain right across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. It is called the “Baltic Way”.
In the EU, 23 August is a day of remembrance for the victims of dictatorships.

teile.einleitung: The Fall of Saigon was the capture of the South Vietnamese capital, Saigon, by North Vietnamese troops on 30 April 1975. It ended the long Vietnam War with a victory for the communists. Shortly before, thousands of people fled the city in a dramatic helicopter rescue operation.
wichtigste: The Fall of Saigon happened on 30 April 1975.
It ended the Vietnam War with victory for the North Vietnamese communists.
American combat troops had already left Vietnam in 1973.
In Operation Frequent Wind, thousands of people were flown out by helicopter at the last minute.
A North Vietnamese tank broke through the gate of the Presidential Palace.
In 1976 Vietnam was united as a single communist state.
Saigon was then renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

abschnitte.text: After the end of French colonial rule, Vietnam was divided into two parts in **1954**. In the north the communists ruled under **Ho Chi Minh**; in the south there was a government supported by the USA. Soon communist troops and rebels, the **Viet Cong**, were fighting against the south. From the mid-1960s the USA sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers to Vietnam.

The war cost a great many lives and was becoming more and more controversial in the USA too. In January **1973** a peace agreement was signed in Paris. The American combat troops then withdrew, but the fighting between north and south went on. Without help from the USA, the South Vietnamese army grew weaker and weaker.

At the beginning of 1975 North Vietnam launched a large offensive and captured one city after another within a few weeks. In April the troops stood outside **Saigon**. On the morning of **30 April 1975** tanks rolled into the city, and one of them broke through the gate of the **Presidential Palace**. The South Vietnamese president Duong Van Minh announced the surrender.

In the last two days before the fall, American helicopters flew thousands of people out of Saigon in **Operation Frequent Wind**. Among other places, they took off from the roof of the American embassy and carried people to ships at sea. It was one of the largest helicopter rescue operations in history. However, many South Vietnamese who wanted to flee had to stay behind.

On 2 July **1976** Vietnam was reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, and Saigon was renamed **Ho Chi Minh City**. Many supporters of the old government were sent to re-education camps. In the following years hundreds of thousands fled across the sea in small boats as **boat people**, and some found a new home in Switzerland. In Vietnam 30 April is a public holiday today, Reunification Day.

begriffe.erklaerung: When one side in a war gives up and yields to the enemy.
Moving people quickly away from a dangerous area.
Communist fighters in South Vietnam who were supported by North Vietnam.
People who fled Vietnam across the sea in small boats after 1975.

gewusst: The tank that broke through the gate of the Presidential Palace is now in a museum in Hanoi.
Because there was not enough room on the ships, some helicopters were simply pushed into the sea after landing.
Many people in Vietnam still use the name Saigon in everyday life.
